eligibility.exact_action_basis: H.R.29 would extend the federal mandatory-custody category to the following offenses: burglary, theft, larceny or shoplifting. The four listed property-offense terms take the meaning assigned by the jurisdiction where the acts occurred. The exact bill adds an INA 236(c) mandatory-custody category requiring inadmissibility under INA 212(a)(6)(A), (6)(C), or (7) together with a specified criminal predicate: being charged, arrested, convicted, admitting commission, or admitting acts constituting the essential elements. These inadmissibility categories concern presence without admission/parole or undesignated arrival, material immigration fraud/false citizenship claims, and specified entry-document defects, subject to their existing statutory qualifications. DHS must issue a detainer for a person meeting the new ground and, if the person is not otherwise detained by Federal, State or local officials, effectively and expeditiously take custody. The bill also gives a State attorney general or other authorized State officer standing, on alleged harm to the State or residents (including financial harm in excess of $100), to seek appropriate injunctive relief in district court over five specified federal matters: INA 235(b)(1)/(2) detention/removal requirements; INA 236 release, bond or parole decisions; the existing INA 243(d) visa-discontinuance requirement for countries denying or unreasonably delaying acceptance; violation of the existing INA 212(d)(5)(A) case-by-case urgent-humanitarian/significant-public-benefit parole limits; and INA 241(a)(2) detention during the removal period. Courts must advance and expedite these cases to the greatest practicable extent. INA 236(e) removes its express release/grant shield while leaving the other printed discretionary-judgment/detention/revocation/denial restrictions, and INA 242(f)(1) receives an exception for the printed listed actions, while its separate final-removal-order injunction standard remains. These review changes do not establish a general right to enjoin every immigration action. The parole clause changes its named administering actor to the Secretary of Homeland Security. The baseline removal period is generally 90 days with specified starting/extension conditions; the bill adds litigation standing over its detention requirement rather than creating that period. The pre-existing narrow protection-release exception remains, redesignated as INA 236(c)(4), including its witness/potential-witness/cooperator and immediate-family/close-associate categories, no-danger/appearance conditions and offense-severity procedure.

The exact House-passed H.R.23 requires the President, not later than 60 days after enactment and on an ongoing basis, to impose sanctions if the ICC is attempting to investigate, arrest, detain or prosecute a protected person. Covered foreign persons are those the President determines directly engage in or aid such an effort; materially assist, sponsor or provide specified support/goods/services for it; or are owned/controlled by, or currently act or purport to have acted for, a person directly engaging in it. For covered aliens, the bill makes them inadmissible, ineligible for visas or other entry documents, admission or parole, and any other INA benefit. Their visas/entry documents must be revoked regardless of issuance date, effective immediately and automatically canceling other valid visas/entry documents in their possession. The immigration sanctions also apply to each sanctioned foreign person's spouse, parent, sibling or adult child; the separate property-blocking requirement applies to the principal foreign persons described in 3(a)(1). Foreign person means someone other than the defined United States person, which includes U.S. citizens, lawful permanent residents, U.S.-organized entities and any person in the United States. The incorporated INA alien definition excludes U.S. citizens and nationals. Protected persons include any defined U.S. person unless the United States both formally consents to ICC jurisdiction and is a Rome Statute party. They also include foreign citizens or lawful residents of a NATO or designated major non-NATO ally that has not consented to ICC jurisdiction or is not a Rome Statute party. The listed military/government personnel are inclusive examples, not the entire protected class. The President may waive sanctions case by case for periods no longer than 90 days each on a reported vital-national-security determination before the waiver takes effect, including the specified detailed rationale and actions by the United States and ICC. The President may terminate sanctions on written certification that the ICC has ceased all covered efforts and permanently closed/withdrawn/ended/terminated them. Imposition also requires congressional briefing/written notice within 10 days. The package includes property blocking under existing IEEPA authorities and penalties, rescission of available ICC appropriations at enactment and a prospective ban on using appropriated funds for the ICC. Immigration membership follows the direct travel/admission/parole/benefit restrictions, not the foreign-affairs findings. These are proposed legislative requirements; existing general INA inadmissibility/temporary-admission authorities are not treated as newly created by this bill. Actual designation, visa revocation, sanctions, enforcement or enactment is not inferred.

The complete January15,2025 H.R.33 House EH passage proposal establishes reciprocal, qualified Taiwan tax relief and a separately governed tax-agreement process. Its personal citizenship/residence predicates are the Immigration overlap candidate; the country name, corporate geography and diplomatic findings alone do not supply eligibility. The general qualified-resident definition requires liability to Taiwan tax by domicile, residence, management, incorporation or a similar criterion AND not being a USperson, determined WITHOUT the new dual-resident tax-treatment rule; corporate entities also face their separate limitations on benefits. Existing7701(a)(30) includes a UScitizen OR resident, with separate partnership/corporation/estate/trust branches. Taiwan citizenship or ancestry alone is not printed as the beneficiary test. The natural-person tax-residence baseline in7701(b) has alternative LPR, substantial-presence and first-year-election routes, with its timing, exempt-individual/presence and closer-connection qualifications. It is not synonymous with immigration status, lawful presence, nationality or visa class.
New894A(c)(3) separately covers an applicable dual resident who is NOT A USCITIZEN, is a USresident determined WITHOUT(c)(3)(E), and would qualify as a Taiwan resident but for the general USperson exclusion. That individual must satisfy ONE of three routes: a permanent home available in Taiwan AND none in the US; permanent homes in BOTH places AND closer personal/economic relations (center of vital interests) to Taiwan; OR the habitual-abode route. The last requires EITHER no permanent home available in either place OR homes in both with an undetermined center of vital interests, AND habitual abode in Taiwan AND NOT the US. The three routes are alternatives, not three cumulative requirements, and Taiwan residence alone does not suffice. Notwithstanding7701, an individual qualifying THROUGH this dual-resident paragraph for all or part of a taxable year is treated as not a USresident ONLY FOR COMPUTING that individual's US INCOME-TAX LIABILITY for that year or portion. This does not itself revoke or confer LPR status, nationality, a visa, INA admission, work authorization or immigration relief, and does not make UScitizens eligible under the dual-resident route. Existing7701(b)(6)'s separate tax treatment after qualified treaty-residence/notification is not an immigration revocation enacted by H.R.33.
The qualified-wage exemption has an ADDITIONAL recipient test: a qualified Taiwan resident must EITHER not be a USresident determined WITHOUT the new dual-resident tax-treatment rule OR be a regular-component crew member of a ship or aircraft in international traffic. Therefore(c)(3)(E)'s income-tax nonresidence does not by itself satisfy the first wage route. Qualified wages must concern personal services performed in the US, be paid by or for an employer OTHER THAN a USperson, AND not be borne by a USpermanent establishment of any person OTHER THAN a USperson. Directors' fees, entertainer/athlete income, student/trainee income, pensions, specified US/State/possession government employment amounts and guidance-specified other amounts are excluded from this wage definition. No exemption for every student, trainee, crew member, noncitizen employee or Taiwan resident is inferred. A separate entertainer/athlete provision concerns own US personal activities, qualified Taiwan residence and annual aggregate gross receipts NOT EXCEEDING $30,000, with its printed qualified-wage-definition and permanent-establishment-income exceptions; it is not a deduction or exclusion of the first $30,000 from unlimited receipts.
For specified interest, dividends, royalties, printed871(a)(1)(C) original-issue-discount amounts and871(a)(1)(D) contingent gains, the proposal substitutes qualified rates in the identified tax/withholding provisions: generally10percent, dividends15percent, and a conditional10percent corporate dividend route with ownership/holding and predecessor rules and RIC/REIT exception. Existing871 and1441 retain other tax/withholding categories and exceptions; the proposal is not a reduction of every tax or every nonresident withholding rate, including the distinct14percent qualified scholarship/fellowship baseline. The special substitution excludes nonqualified REIT dividends (the printed publicly traded class and not-more-than5percent holding definition matters), amounts subject to897, payments from defined expatriated entities to foreign related persons, and860C-included income to the extent of the specified REMIC excess inclusion. The material897,7874 and860C operative baselines preserve real-property, entity/related-person and residual-interest context; no particular holding, transaction or taxpayer is adjudicated. Existing benefits, taxes and exclusions are not represented as all newly created or repealed.
The proposal also replaces the specified business-tax connection with its defined USpermanent-establishment connection, retains taxes on effectively connected taxable income under the printed sections, modifies the real-property treatment and supplies a corporate branch-profits rate/connection change. The printed wage/other-income and entertainer-conduit exceptions, contractually-authorized designation exception, partnership/estate/trust attribution and rules similar to894(c) for hybrid payments remain. Its establishment definition preserves fixed-place and habitual binding-contract routes, more-than12-month project/rig/ship rule with qualifying connected-person periods, preparatory/auxiliary/storage/processing exclusions and ordinary-course independent-agent exception. A USsubsidiary/control relationship alone does not establish the parent's USpermanent establishment. Corporate ownership/income, publicly traded and qualified-subsidiary alternatives, qualifying intermediaries, qualified-payment exclusions and the separately limited active-business item route are tax/entity qualifications, not immigration status of every owner or employee. Their printed foreign-country-of-concern reference is not a new personal nationality-wide bar. This candidate does not purport to calculate every corporate tax, REMIC excess inclusion, connected-person ownership or taxpayer liability, or independently audit the entire incorporated tax code.
NONE of new894A applies for a period unless Treasury determines Taiwan has provided reciprocal benefits to USpersons for that period. Presidential/designee letters, agreements or other necessary/appropriate steps are authorized; actual reciprocity, negotiations, agreement, implementation, exemption or savings are not established by this House vote. Treasury guidance authority covers establishment/income, abuse prevention, records/reporting, qualified-resident/withholding proof, predecessor stock, wages/entertainment, ownership and application dates; dates MAY differ for source withholding and other taxes. Guidance must be consistent with the February7,2016 USmodel income-tax convention TO THE EXTENT PRACTICAL, not an automatic incorporation of every model article or current treaty benefit.
TitleII authorizes negotiating/entering an agreement only AFTER that reciprocity determination, confines its elements to the printed customary-bilateral/model-convention scope while permitting restatement of existing double-tax law/agreements, and retains congressional approval/implementing legislation plus Taiwan approval/implementation confirmation for entry into force. Written commencement notification is at least15calendar days BEFORE negotiations; an initial briefing is due within90days AFTER commencement, then every180days until entry into the agreement, with requested meetings and ongoing consultation. Contemplated text must be publicly posted at least60days BEFORE entering the agreement. Final text/technical explanation and implementation-policy submissions have separate270-day AFTER-entry triggers. The specified approval text and Senate ForeignRelations/Finance versus House WaysAndMeans referrals remain distinct. Inconsistent agreement or approval provisions have no effect against the IRC; this title does not implicitly amend other law or limit other authority except as specifically provided. The process applies separately to each subsequent supplemental/superseding agreement after the specified enactments. Findings and policy statements are not observed diplomatic or economic outcomes.
One whole H.R.33 passage choice and one episode are projected from unchanged governed Clerk observations. Yea supports and Nay opposes the complete qualified tax-relief/agreement proposal; neither establishes a separate component stance, motive, immigration outcome or preferred alternative. Exact EH and2024 baseline labels remain; no universal later-law currency or individual legal/tax advice is claimed. This is a defensible direct personal-status overlap candidate under existing cross-case standards, routed for independent domain/application review, without new ontology acceptance, editorial approval, publication or production eligibility.

The exact House-passed H.R.30 adds INA 212(a)(2)(J) inadmissibility for a person convicted of, admitting commission of, or admitting acts constituting the essential elements of a sex offense under 34 USC 20911(5), or a conspiracy to commit one. New 212(a)(2)(K) uses those same conviction/admission predicates for a crime of domestic violence (defined through 237(a)(2)(E)), stalking, child abuse/neglect/abandonment, or a crime violating the protective-order portion addressing credible threats, repeated harassment or bodily injury. The INA baseline makes these inadmissibility grounds relevant to visas and admission; the bill is not limited by its title to persons unlawfully present. It separately adds INA 237(a)(2)(G) deportability for conviction of a defined sex offense or conspiracy: admission of conduct alone is not the predicate in this new deportability clause. The existing 237(a)(2)(E)(i) after-admission conviction ground for domestic violence, stalking and child abuse/neglect/abandonment remains; its domestic-violence definition is expanded to include any crime constituting domestic violence under 34 USC 12291(a), regardless of whether the jurisdiction receives grants. Noncriminal behavior mentioned in the victim-services portion of that definition is not itself converted into a crime by this bill. The incorporated sex-offense definition covers criminal sexual-act/contact offenses, specified offenses against minors, listed federal/military offenses, and attempts/conspiracies, with its foreign-conviction fairness and consensual-conduct limitations. The latter exclude specified consensual adult conduct unless custodial authority exists, and specified conduct where the victim is at least 13 and the offender is not more than 4 years older. Some covered conduct already can trigger existing criminal inadmissibility or deportability grounds; these are additional grounds and a definition expansion, not the creation of all immigration consequences for these crimes. INA 101(a)(48) supplies the existing conviction framework, including specified withheld adjudications with a guilt/plea/facts predicate plus court-ordered punishment, penalty or restraint. H.R.30 references 20911(5), rather than expressly importing the separate 20911(8) juvenile-conviction definition. The bill leaves the 237(a)(7) discretionary battered-person waiver for specified domestic-violence/stalking/protective-order deportability grounds intact; that waiver is not written to cover the new sex-offense ground. Existing 212(d)(3) discretionary temporary nonimmigrant admission and 212(d)(13)/(14) T/U status waiver authorities remain within their own conditions. Existing 212(h) enumerates other criminal grounds and is not expanded to the newJ/K grounds. No universal waiver or automatic removal is established. The new 237(a)(2) deportability ground sits within the existing 237(a) framework for an alien (including a crewman) in and admitted to the United States, with removal upon the specified government order. It is not a universal new deportability ground for every unadmitted alien. INA 101 distinguishes immigration admission (lawful entry after inspection/authorization) from admitting criminal conduct; parole alone is not admission. This governing status scope is separate from any offense's after-admission timing element. No individual admission status or actual removal order is inferred.

The exact amendment No.2 in Part B of House Report 119-2, offered by Trahan as Pettersen's designee, would replace the applicability paragraph with a condition on THIS ACT AND ALL AMENDMENTS MADE BY THIS ACT taking effect on the date the Secretary of Health and Human Services AND the Attorney General jointly certify IN THE FEDERAL REGISTER that this Act will lead to a reduction in overdose deaths. The condition is global, including the proposed statutory class-control predicate incorporated by the identified Immigration grounds, and is not confined to one scheduling clause. It is not certification by either official alone, an observed reduction in deaths, a mandatory certification date or a change to the existing temporary control. The amendment FAILED and the condition was not adopted. Yea supports adding this condition; Nay opposes adding it, without establishing a position on whole-bill passage or a preferred alternative. The adopted rule's Part A technical corrections and this rejected Part B condition remain distinct.
The Immigration relationship is confined to the controlled-substance classification expressly incorporated by the identified grounds, rather than every criminal-law consequence. Under existing 8 U.S.C. 1182(a), subject to the chapter's exceptions, aliens inadmissible under the listed paragraphs are ineligible for visas and admission. Section 1182(a)(2)(A)(i)(II) retains conviction, admission of committing the offense, or admission of acts constituting its essential elements; a violation, conspiracy or attempt to violate a State, United States or foreign law or regulation relating to a controlled substance defined in 21 U.S.C. 802 is still required. The youth and petty-crime exceptions printed in clause (ii) apply to the moral-turpitude branch in clause (i)(I), not automatically to this controlled-substance branch. Section 1182(a)(2)(C)(i) separately requires the consular officer or Attorney General to know or have reason to believe the alien is or has been an illicit trafficker, knowing aider, abettor, assister, conspirator or colluder, or has endeavored to engage in the specified trafficking; it includes the separately printed listed-chemical alternative and does not substitute a conviction requirement for these tests. Clause (C)(ii) is governed by the SAME common governmental threshold: the consular officer or Attorney General must know or have reason to believe that the applicant is the spouse, son or daughter of an alien inadmissible under (C)(i), has obtained within the previous five years a financial or other benefit from that alien's illicit activity, and knew or reasonably should have known that the benefit came from that illicit activity. The governmental threshold and the recipient's own knowledge conditions are distinct and both remain; relationship alone does not suffice.
Under 8 U.S.C. 1227(a), an alien, including an alien crewman, IN AND ADMITTED TO THE UNITED STATES is subject to removal UPON THE ORDER OF THE ATTORNEY GENERAL if within a listed deportable class. Its controlled-substance conviction ground in 1227(a)(2)(B)(i) separately requires conviction at any time after admission for a violation, conspiracy or attempt to violate the identified State, United States or foreign law or regulation relating to a substance defined by 21 U.S.C. 802, except a single offense involving possession for one's own use of 30 grams or less of marijuana. Neither classification alone nor this House choice establishes an individual's deportability or produces an automatic removal order. The separate drug-abuser/addict ground in (B)(ii) is not given an express section 802 incorporation that it does not print. Existing 1182(h) allows only its separately qualified discretionary waiver, with the controlled-substance part confined to a single simple-possession offense involving 30 grams or less of marijuana and its other eligibility, exclusions and discretion preserved. Section 1182(d)(3)(A) separately permits qualified temporary nonimmigrant admission in the Attorney General's discretion, with recommendation/approval or documentation requirements and its printed exclusions and conditions; this is not an all-drug immigrant waiver or an entitlement. These grounds and waivers are not newly enacted or repealed by this proposal.
Section 802(6) defines a controlled substance through inclusion in Schedules I-V. The February 6, 2025 baseline already included temporary Schedule I class control under 21 C.F.R. 1308.11(h)(30). The original order ran February 6, 2018-February 6, 2020; Public Law 116-114 kept it in effect notwithstanding other law, and the April 2020 correction expressly preserved uninterrupted control despite the electronic-CFR omission, distinguishing effectiveness from applicability. The latest pre-vote extension in Public Law 118-158 section 5105 continued that order through March 31, 2025. H.R.27 would ADD statutory Schedule I coverage without that temporary March 31 expiry, under its own definition and exceptions. It does not say it repeals or replaces temporary paragraph (h)(30), establish first-ever class control, or make every listed substance's status irrevocable. The source-supported proposed continuation of an expressly incorporated classification is the bounded domain mechanism; no universal criminal-law or collateral-consequence domain rule is accepted.
The temporary order prints isomers, esters, ethers, salts and salts of those forms, excluding substances under another DEA Controlled Substance Code Number and those with an FDA section 505 exemption or approval. H.R.27's proposed Schedule I(e)(1) instead prints its own material/compound/mixture/preparation and salts/isomers/salts-of-isomers language, unless specifically exempted or in another schedule. Its definition uses one or more of five specified structural modifications: phenyl-portion replacement in the phenethyl group, listed substitution in/on that group, listed substitution in/on the piperidine ring, replacement of the aniline ring with an aromatic monocycle, or replacement of the N-propionyl group by another acyl group. Paragraph (e)(3) excludes substances controlled by Attorney General action under section 201 or expressly listed in another schedule; the temporary FDA phrase is not repeated verbatim. The proposed class and temporary class are not declared identical chemical sets, and no particular medicine or substance is classified here. Medical fentanyl's existing Schedule II listing remains distinct; this is not moving all fentanyl into Schedule I. Existing scheduling/removal authority and the proposal's exemptions remain. An optional Attorney General list does not determine the status of every qualifying substance; absence from that list does not negate statutory control under the proposed definition.
The global effectiveness condition would gate the proposed class coverage and the Act's other amendments, including research-registration, technical dispensing and specified penalty amendments. The amendment does not rewrite every separately printed enactment-relative deadline or establish an actual lapse in control. The separate passage vote is not this amendment choice. The existing temporary baseline, independent offense/admission/knowledge/timing/exception predicates, and individual removal-order requirement remain; no certification, enforcement result, personal legal finding, component preference, motive or enactment is inferred.

The exact H.R.27 EH passage choice includes the adopted Part A technical corrections and adds statutory Schedule I(e) coverage for the defined fentanyl-related substances WITHOUT the temporary March 31, 2025 expiry, subject to its own definition and exceptions. It does NOT repeal or replace temporary 21 C.F.R.1308.11(h)(30). This proposes a source-qualified continuation of the controlled-substance classification expressly used by specified Immigration grounds; it is not the first control of the class, a claim of identical chemical sets, or an automatic personal immigration outcome. The failed Part B joint-certification amendment was not adopted. Under section 7(a), the amendments apply from enactment irrespective of finalized rules.

The complete passage proposal also changes qualified research-registration procedures: an expedited route for investigational-exemption or specified HHS/Defense/VA-conducted/funded research, distinct notice/application timelines for already-registered and unregistered researchers, stated quantities and supplemental notices, and the preserved controlled-substance import/export requirements. It provides conditional shared institutional registration, qualified same-city/county sites under one institutional control with notices, inspection changes while retaining necessary anti-diversion inspections, conditional continuation after new Schedule I placement and specified hearing/application steps, small-quantity manufacturing incident to research with a marijuana-growing exclusion, and transparency for special research procedures. Those are not all researchers exempted from registration, unrestricted manufacturing or a new immigration admission rule. Technical dispensing-reference corrections, Attorney General rulemaking within six months with interim-final-rule/comment/hearing provisions, specified insertions of fentanyl-related substances into 21 U.S.C.841(b)(1) and 960(b) penalty provisions, and the section 802(60) class-definition cross-reference remain parts of the whole choice. Section 7(b) is a rule of construction concerning analogue treatment for those penalty provisions and pre-enactment conduct, not an automatic retroactive INA finding. The McCray reference is a sense-of-Congress statement, not proof of an actual case outcome. Yea or Nay concerns the WHOLE proposal, without identifying a separate component preference, motive or preferred alternative; the House result does not establish enactment, certification, a particular substance's classification, inadmissibility, deportability, removal or a realized health/enforcement effect.

The exact House-passed H.R.35 adds 18 USC 40B: operating a motor vehicle within 100 miles of the United States border while intentionally fleeing a pursuing U.S. Border Patrol agent acting under lawful authority, or a pursuing Federal/State/local officer actively assisting or under Border Patrol command. The ordinary penalty alternatives are imprisonment up to 2 years, a title 18 fine, or both; where serious bodily injury results the imprisonment alternative is 5–20 years, and where any person's death results it is 10 years to life, with fine-or-both alternatives retained in both cases. The bill adds INA 212(a)(2)(J) inadmissibility and 237(a)(2)(G) deportability for any alien convicted of, admitting commission of, or admitting acts constituting the essential elements of 40B(a). It also inserts 208A making a person meeting that same predicate ineligible for relief under the immigration laws, expressly including asylum under 208. Neither arrest alone nor merely being within 100 miles is the printed immigration predicate. Pre-existing 18 USC 758 already criminalizes vehicle flight/evasion from an immigration or other federal checkpoint followed by fleeing law-enforcement agents above the legal speed limit, with up-to 5 years/fine/both; existing 237(a)(2)(A)(iv) already makes a conviction for 758 deportable. H.R.35 creates a different officer/geography/intent predicate and additional immigration consequences, rather than the first-ever immigration checkpoint-flight offense or deportability ground. Unlike that existing deportability ground, the newG also accepts specified admissions. Existing INA 101(a)(48) conviction rules remain. The Attorney General, with the Secretary of Homeland Security, must report annually to both Judiciary Committees on violations, charged/apprehended/not-charged/not-apprehended counts, and penalties sought/imposed. A reporting duty is not evidence of actual violations, convictions or enforcement. The separate broad relief-bar clause is preserved as printed; it is not replaced by a blanket claim that existing narrow waivers guarantee relief, and no individual asylum or removal outcome is decided. The new 237(a)(2) deportability ground sits within the existing 237(a) framework for an alien (including a crewman) in and admitted to the United States, with removal upon the specified government order. It is not a universal new deportability ground for every unadmitted alien. INA 101 distinguishes immigration admission (lawful entry after inspection/authorization) from admitting criminal conduct; parole alone is not admission. This governing status scope is separate from any offense's after-admission timing element. No individual admission status or actual removal order is inferred.

The exact H.R.495 EH proposal adds “and annually thereafter” to Public Law 117-263 section 7134(a)(2), after “development of the strategic plan”. The Commissioner of U.S. Customs and Border Protection would therefore report on implementation of the existing counter illicit cross-border tunnel operations strategic plan not later than one year after its development and annually thereafter, to the House Homeland Security and Senate Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Committees. The pre-existing 7134(a)(1) already requires the Commissioner, coordinating with the DHS Science and Technology Under Secretary and appropriate DHS officials, to develop the plan within 180 days of the 2022law. Its existing scope includes risk-based identification/breach/assessment/remediation criteria, technologies and community impacts, information sharing, Border Patrol sector indicators and technology/staffing needs. H.R.495 changes the reporting cadence, not those plan requirements. The separate 6 USC 257 annual report on discovered Mexico–U.S. tunnels and DHS prevention/investigation/prosecution needs already exists and is not the provision amended here. Existing 7134(b) authorized$1 million for each of fiscal 2023 and 2024 for plan development and remediation; H.R.495 neither extends that authorization nor supplies new appropriations. Membership follows direct border-tunnel operations reporting. Actual reporting, tunnel remediation, border outcomes or enactment are not established by the House suspension-and-passage vote.

The exact H.R.993 EH proposal requires the DHS Secretary, acting through the CBP Commissioner and DHS Science and Technology Under Secretary, to submit a plan within 180 days of enactment to the House Homeland Security and Senate Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Committees. The plan is to identify, integrate and deploy emerging/advanced technologies to enhance or address gaps in border-security operations. Its prescribed contents cover innovation-team use and composition, contributions and coordination, technologies from other agencies, procurement authorities and need for alternatives, scaling programs, program goals/timelines, border-community privacy/security impacts, replacement costs, research/private-sector coordination, metrics and listed aircraft/surveillance/inspection/tunnel/communications technologies. The bill gives the CBP Commissioner express authority to maintain one or more innovation teams to research and adapt new/emerging commercial technologies for border capability gaps and urgent mission needs, and assess potential outcomes including negative consequences where documented gaps are yet to be determined. It requires each maintained team to establish operating procedures, defined roles/partner relationships and transition protocols, plus strategic planning with costs, timeframes, metrics and performance parameters, including technology-transition rates. The Commissioner must report within 180 days and annually thereafter to the same committees on team procedures/plans, technologies piloted in the preceding fiscal year, success/gap determinations and status of transitioning successful technologies. This provides statutory authority and prescribed planning/reporting for maintaining teams; it does not establish that innovation teams or pilots first come into existence with this proposal. The technology list and planned deployment goals are not universal mandates to deploy every technology. No appropriation, universal pilot success or actual operational outcome is stated. Membership follows the express direct border-operations scope rather than DHS administration alone.

The exact March 11, 2025 House choice is passage of the complete H.R. 1968 continuing-appropriations and extensions package. The selected, separately source-bound Immigration mechanisms here include DHS funding and retained safeguards, division A section 11208(a) refugee and adjustment date amendments, the separate section 11208(b) Afghan-program heading amendment, and incorporated physician, E-Verify, religious-worker and H-2B rules with reserved timing application. Other Immigration components of the package remain under review; this candidate does not claim complete component coverage.

Section 11208(a)(1) would add fiscal year 2025 to section 599D(b)(3). Within refugee admissions already allocated under section 207(a)(3) for nationals of the independent states of the former Soviet Union, Estonia, Latvia and Lithuania, the President must allocate one thousand admissions to the narrower section 599D(b)(2)(B) recipient category. That category consists of people who are or were nationals of those countries, are current members of the Ukrainian Catholic Church or Ukrainian Orthodox Church, and demonstrate public, active and continuous participation (or attempted participation) in the religious activities of that church. The larger nationality-based admissions allocation and this narrower religious recipient category are distinct. It is not an extra one thousand outside the allocated admissions ceiling, and it does not increase the general refugee admission ceiling. Replacing 2024 with 2025 in all three section 599D(e) branches would carry forward the special category-based fear showing (asserting a well-founded fear and a credible basis for concern about possible persecution) for applications submitted before October 1, 2025, the written-reasons requirement to the maximum extent feasible for decisions made before that date, and the specified previously denied applicants' reapplication route before that date. The complete baseline keeps its distinct former-Soviet/Baltic, Vietnam/Laos/Cambodia and Iranian religious-minority category definitions and other refugee admission qualifications. Neither country membership alone nor a reduced fear-showing rule guarantees admission.

Section 11208(a)(2) would change the section 599E(b)(2) qualifying inspection-and-parole window's ending date from September 30, 2024 to September 30, 2025, retaining the August 15, 1988 starting date. Its separate national list covers former-Soviet states, Estonia, Latvia, Lithuania, Vietnam, Laos and Cambodia; the Iranian category in 599D is not imported into this adjustment route. The person must have been denied refugee status before the qualifying inspection and parole, apply for adjustment, have at least one year of physical presence and be physically present on filing, satisfy the remaining admissibility and qualified waiver rules, and pay the prescribed fee. The baseline's admission-record date and no-visa-offset rules remain. Extending the parole window is not a new universal parole power, automatic permanent residence, or an extension of every person's adjustment filing deadline.

Section 11208(b) changes only the terminal year in the heading of Afghan Allies Protection Act section 602(b)(3)(F), from 2024 to 2025. It does not amend that paragraph's printed operative visa-number limit, employment-period endpoint, Chief-of-Mission application deadline or exhaustion rule. Those are distinct from the heading and retain their own complete captured qualifications; the candidate does not declare a new visa quota or a new application deadline from this heading edit. The same outer section's Israel loan-guarantee and stockpile amendments are separate fiscal/foreign-assistance context, not personal immigration mechanisms.

Division A sections 1101-1107 would continue the applicable fiscal year 2024 account levels, transfers, obligation limitations, authorities and conditions, subject to the exact listed exceptions and later overrides. DHS division C sections 543-546 are expressly excluded; their old rescissions are not repeated as retained provisions. September 30, 2025 is the default end date, subject to otherwise-provided availability; multi-year and no-year appropriations retain comparable periods. Earlier continuing-resolution expenditures are charged to the applicable funding, not added again. This is not an unrestricted new enforcement authority or permission to restart prohibited activities.

Section 1701(1) sets the ICE operations/support level at $9,986,542,000, replacing the $9,501,542,000 baseline level. The baseline's at least $5,082,218,000 enforcement/detention/removal allocation, including unaccompanied-minor transportation, remains a distinct minimum within a mixed-use account; the account also funds forced-child-labor and intellectual-property enforcement and other specified activities. The complete account total is not assigned solely to removals or detention, and no actual spending or additional sum on top of earlier continuing-resolution expenditures is inferred. CBP operations/support retains the $18,426,870,000 baseline level with its mixed border, customs and other functions. Its $650,000,000 transfer to FEMA for non-Federal sheltering and related activities to relieve CBP short-term holding overcrowding is within that amount, with the $9,100,000 FEMA administrative-cost cap; it is not an extra amount outside the CBP level. USCIS operations/support continues at $271,140,000 for specified operations including E-Verify, refugee/international operations and backlog reduction, additional to other funding without requiring a reduction of the described fees; its $10,000,000 citizenship/integration grant account remains separate.

Section 1706(8) rescinds $2,514,000 of USCIS operations/support unobligated balances made available under the particular section 505 carryover authority. That baseline authority concerns at most 50 percent of fiscal year 2024 operations/support unobligated balances, recorded at notification no later than June 30, 2025, retaining their account/purpose through September 30, 2025 and requiring section 503 notification before obligation. The rescission is not a repeal of all current USCIS funding or fee revenue. Printed fiscal-year and notification language is retained; no blanket year substitution or adjudication of actual balances, notifications or spending is made. Section 1705 removes section 227's force for fiscal year 2025; section 227 is a towing-vessel inspection-fee funding restriction with its own conditions, not an immigration detention safeguard. No actual vessel fee or fee liability is adjudicated.

Retained section 207 bars a defined new universal pedestrian/cyclist/private-vehicle border-crossing fee at northern or southern land ports and studies of imposing it; it does not abolish every existing border-related fee. Under section 212, ICE operations/support funds cannot continue a section 287(g) delegation after the DHS Inspector General determines the governing agreement was materially violated. The complete 1357(g) baseline keeps qualified written state/local agreements, training and federal direction/supervision, specified powers and duration, voluntary participation and separate communication/cooperation savings; no agreement violation or local actor's liability is inferred. Section 213 restricts those same ICE account funds for continuation of detention contracts when both of the two most recent overall facility evaluations are below adequate or its subsequent-system equivalent median score; those evaluations are conducted by ICE's Office of Professional Responsibility, not the Inspector General. Neither provision establishes that any particular agreement or facility fails its condition.

Retained sections 527-529 constrain use of the covered DHS funds: congressional oversight access cannot be obstructed or staged by temporary changes, Members need no prior notice, and designated staff may be required to request access 24 hours ahead. The restraint funding bar covers a woman who is pregnant or in post-delivery recuperation. The printed subsection (b) exceptions are phrased for a pregnant woman: an individualized serious-flight-risk or immediate-serious-harm determination where other means cannot prevent the risk, or a medical professional responsible for her care determining therapeutic restraints appropriate for her medical safety. When a pregnant woman is restrained under those exceptions, only the safest and least restrictive restraints determined by the appropriate treating medical professional may be used. Active labor or delivery is an absolute restraint bar; specified positions and constricting restraints are prohibited, with left-side positioning to the maximum feasible extent. Custody death, potential sexual assault/abuse and specified misconduct-allegation records cannot be destroyed with the covered funds; disclosure to a person charged, segregated or otherwise punished for such an allegation requires that person's request and the applicable law, regulations and litigation disclosure rules. These are funding restrictions with retained qualifications, not findings that mistreatment occurred or unconditional disclosure rights.

Retained section 538 requires bimonthly southwest-border arrival estimates covering the current and following fiscal years, with single-adult/family-unit/unaccompanied-child breakdowns, independent validation/verification, interagency sharing and specified planning/budget uses. If the required estimates are not provided for the described purposes, section 503 reprogramming/transfer authority is suspended until the required estimates reach the appropriations committees. Section 540 requires an alternatives and cost-benefit analysis before DHS requests Defense border-security support, a report within 30 days of the request, and another within 30 days after support is granted with quarterly reports during assistance. These requirements do not establish actual arrivals, agency noncompliance, a deployment, or an independently voted preference for military border assistance.

The DHS incorporation in section 1101(a)(6) expressly includes 2024 division G sections 102-105. Their complete printed clauses and material statutory baselines are separately bound. Section 1105's general continuance and section 1106's default September 30, 2025 endpoint are also preserved. The application of that continuance to the incorporated provisions' own September 30, 2024 substitutions and fiscal-year-2024 H-2B conditions is separately reserved for source-grounded review; this candidate neither silently changes their dates nor declares those authorities ineffective solely from the old printed year.

Incorporated section 102 applies a September 30, 2024 substitution to technical-corrections section 220(c), whose applicability sentence concerns persons admitted in J exchange-visitor status or acquiring that status after admission before the specified date. This is not a universal deadline for every physician-waiver application. Complete 1182(e) and 1184(l) retain the qualified two-year foreign-residence waiver framework: favorable recommendation and public-interest finding, the applicable interested agency request and contractual-country no-objection condition, a state-request maximum of 30 per fiscal year, full-time employment with a 90-day start and at least three-year service conditions, shortage-area/specialty requirements with their Veterans Affairs, medical-research/training and up-to-ten state facility exceptions. The qualified change to H-1B status has its own numerical-limit exception; failure to fulfill the contract or continuing public-interest/service conditions retains the stated foreign-residence consequences. No particular physician qualifies or receives a waiver from this incorporation alone.

Incorporated section 103 substitutes the printed September 30, 2024 date in IIRIRA section 401(b)'s program-termination clause. It does not create a universal mandatory E-Verify requirement. The complete 401-405 baseline keeps generally voluntary participation with specific federal-government, legislative-branch and qualifying-violation-order exceptions. Identity/employment confirmation has its own inquiry and secondary-verification process: a tentative nonconfirmation may be contested and is not treated as a final finding of unauthorized employment. Employment cannot be terminated because of failed confirmation until nonconfirmation becomes final, without barring termination for another reason. Continued employment after final nonconfirmation has distinct notification and rebuttable-presumption rules; the candidate does not infer actual ineligibility, mandatory dismissal of every person, system accuracy or employer liability.

Incorporated section 104 applies the printed September 30, 2024 substitution to both non-minister paths in 1101(a)(27)(C)(ii)(II) and (III). The separate minister path in (I) is not given a new date by borrowing the non-minister clauses. The complete definition retains two years of qualifying denomination membership immediately before application, the bona fide nonprofit organization and requested professional/religious-vocation or occupation conditions, continuous prior qualifying work, and the qualified accompanying/following spouse-and-child relationship. It is not permission for every religious worker or a change to every special-immigrant quota.

Incorporated section 105 permits, rather than mandates, a supplemental H-2B increase after DHS consultation with Labor and a determination that the printed fiscal-year-2024 United States business needs cannot be met by willing, qualified and able United States workers for temporary nonagricultural labor. Its increase is bounded by the highest number of H-2B returning-worker-program participants in any fiscal year when those workers were exempt, not an unlimited allotment or an automatic exemption for every returning worker. Complete 1184(g) separately retains the ordinary 66,000 principal-worker annual cap, spouse/child distinction, petition-order and other conditional rules, and the 33,000 first-six-month limit; no precise supplemental count, actual discretionary increase or resolved FY2025 application is inferred. Complete 1101(H) retains the temporary nonagricultural category's foreign-residence, labor-availability and medical-graduate exclusion conditions. This remains a whole-package House passage choice, not a separate vote for any program, employer or applicant.

The retained DHS reporting clauses are distinct obligations with different actors and subjects. Section 215 continues semimonthly public detention reporting through complete 2021 section 216 and 2020 section 218. The ICE Director's report must be downloadable, searchable and sortable, with at least the preceding twelve months of semimonthly data. The continued fields include detention population and book-ins; lengths of stay, transfers, stated fear determinations and notices to appear; alternatives-to-detention enrollment and supervision; facility information, classification/threat/criminality data, inspection results and guaranteed capacity; and releases and removals. The stated single-adult/family and facility disaggregations remain. These are reporting requirements, not observed counts, a new credible-fear decision rule or permission to classify an individual from the report alone.

Complete 2021 section 216 also retains the reporting-period-end average stay for people still detained, including its stated post-determination subset, and the printed detention-duration bins: over two years, over one year to two years, over six months to one year, and less than six months. The candidate preserves those exact endpoints rather than filling unstated boundary cases. Its additional field literally concerns the number of individuals described in 28 CFR 115.5, including use and duration of solitary confinement. Complete historical 115.5 defines numerous custody, staff, facility and gender terms; the appropriation does not name a selected definition. The reporting cohort is separately reserved for source-grounded application review. This candidate selects neither only transgender/intersex people nor every person mentioned in that regulation, and it does not extend all of part 115 through a single definitions reference. Semimonthly is retained; no biweekly schedule or new seven-day initial deadline is inferred from the older baseline.

Section 216 separately reapplies complete 2020 section 217. That agreement report is submitted by the ICE Director, not the Inspector General, to the appropriations committees and posted publicly. Its enumerated fields are participating jurisdictions' community outreach, individuals placed in removal proceedings, state/local officer performance including nationality and criminality, and future agreement-expansion plans. There is no enumerated training-report requirement. The retained report's own 45-day timing is preserved alongside general continuance without assigning an unsupported new deadline. Current section 217 is a different 45-day obligation plan submitted by the ICE Chief Financial Officer, delineated by level II program, project and activity. Neither report is the Inspector General's material-agreement-violation trigger. No actual agreement outcome, violation, report delivery, facility condition or solitary-confinement use is asserted.

The retained CBP procurement controls remain qualified by their own funding scope. Section 208 requires the Commissioner to provide an expenditure plan for current and prior procurement/construction/improvement amounts within its printed 90-day period, and bars obligation of the current Act's covered amounts before that plan. Section 209 applies the complete 2021 fencing restriction to funds made available in this Act: Santa Ana Wildlife Refuge, Bentsen-Rio Grande Valley State Park, La Lomita Historical park, the National Butterfly Center, within or east of the Vista del Mar Ranch tract, and historic cemeteries. It is not a prohibition on every border project or every other funding stream. Section 210 permits alteration of National Targeting Center operations but bars reductions of anticipated or planned vetting at existing locations using the specified current, prior-available and fee funds unless specifically authorized by a later statute. No actual project, plan submission or vetting reduction is inferred.

Section 211 earmarks $850,170,000 within the CBP procurement account across separate purposes: $283,500,000 for border-security technologies, $380,900,000 for trade/travel assets and infrastructure, $92,114,000 for facility construction/improvements, $75,983,000 for integrated-operations assets/infrastructure, and $17,673,000 for mission support/infrastructure. This mixed allocation is not an all-wall-construction amount or a claim of actual expenditure. General continuance and the exact printed fiscal-year and availability qualifications remain; no blanket year substitution is performed.

Section 214 permits reprogramming within and transfers to ICE operations/support as necessary for detention of people prioritized for removal, without the time and condition limitation of section 503(d). This is a specific subsection exception, not removal of all transfer caps, advance notices, appropriations conditions or custody safeguards. Complete section 503 separately retains its ordinary reprogramming notification thresholds, transfer caps and exceptions. Its subsection (f) permits up to $20,000,000 to the Immigration Emergency Fund notwithstanding subsection (c), with at least five days' advance appropriations-committee notice. The complete fund baseline authorizes appropriations sufficient for a $35,000,000 balance; it does not establish that balance or actual transfers. General emergency withdrawals require the stated Presidential determination and certification. Paragraph (2) separately permits application-based state/local reimbursement for qualifying requested assistance under its asylum-increase, resident-endangerment or other Attorney General circumstances, with a $20,000,000 aggregate locality cap and a 15-day application-decision rule. That paragraph expressly does not require the paragraph (1) immigration-emergency determination. The transfer ceiling and the separate reimbursement ceiling are not combined into an automatic $40,000,000 allotment; no emergency, reimbursement entitlement or payment is found.

The complete fee-account baseline qualifies the already-bound USCIS additional-funding provision. Section 1356(m) permits fee levels to recover adjudication/naturalization service costs, including similar no-charge asylum or other immigrant services and fee-administration costs; it retains the Virgin Islands and Guam payment provisions. Section 1356(n) keeps deposits available until expended for the described reimbursement of service and fee-administration appropriations. The continuing USCIS appropriation does not require fee reductions; neither that saving nor this baseline fixes a new applicant fee, abolishes fees, converts the account to expiring annual funds or establishes an actual charge.

Retained section 403 permits covered USCIS Federal funds to collect and use biometrics taken at a USCIS Application Support Center overseen virtually by USCIS personnel using appropriate technology. The location and supervision conditions remain. It is not permission for unrestricted home collection, a universal remote-biometric mandate, or a determination of any applicant's eligibility. These remain components of one House package passage choice.

Retained section 512 bars using funds made available in this Act to amend the naturalization oath in INA section 337 (8 USC 1448). It is a funding restriction on amendment, not a new oath, an applicant's eligibility determination or removal of the existing oath's accommodations. The complete baseline retains the qualified religious-training-and-belief accommodations for bearing arms or military service, the child-understanding waiver in its specified naturalization route, and the waiver for inability to understand or communicate understanding because of physical/developmental disability or mental impairment. Their stated showings and official determinations remain; the candidate does not grant a waiver to any person. Public ceremony, title-renunciation and qualified expedited-administration rules remain distinct.

Retained section 514 bars the current Act's funds for planning, testing, piloting or developing a national identification card. It does not abolish all existing identification documents, prohibit every identification-related activity using other funds or establish any person's documentary requirements. Retained section 517 separately bars using the current Act's funds to employ workers described in INA section 274A(h)(3). That definition is employment-specific at the particular time: the person is neither lawfully admitted for permanent residence nor otherwise authorized for that employment under the Act or by the stated authority. This is not a bar on employing every noncitizen, every visa holder or every asylum applicant. No person's actual authorization, employment violation, fee or naturalization outcome is inferred from these package provisions.

The retained sponsor-information protection has its own broad funding but narrow action and information scope. Complete 2024 section 216 applies the terms of 2020 sections 216 and 217. Retained 2020 section 216(a) bars the Secretary of Homeland Security from using funds provided by this Act or any other Act, or the specified Treasury fee accounts available to funded components, to detain, remove, refer for a decision whether to initiate removal proceedings, or initiate removal proceedings against a sponsor, potential sponsor or household member of either, based on information shared by the Secretary of Health and Human Services. It is not limited to one ICE annual account, a ban on every enforcement action from every information source, or a grant of blanket arrest/prosecution immunity. No actual HHS sharing, enforcement decision, sponsor approval or protected person's status is inferred.

The complete subsection (b) removes that funding protection when a background check reveals one of three distinct routes. The first is a felony conviction or pending felony charge relating to an aggravated felony, child abuse, sexual violence or abuse, or child pornography; a pending charge is not recast as a conviction. The second is an association with a business employing a minor unrelated to the sponsor/potential sponsor/household member, where the minor is not paid a legal wage or cannot attend school due to the employment. Both the unrelated-minor condition and the wage-or-school alternatives remain. It is not an exception for every business association, every employed minor or only unpaid work. The third is an association with the organization or implementation of prostitution. The second and third routes do not gain an invented felony-conviction prerequisite. An exception makes the subsection (a) funding protection inapplicable on its stated conditions; it does not order detention or establish that other legal grounds for removal exist.

The incorporated child definition requires no lawful immigration status in the United States and age under eighteen, together with either no parent/legal guardian in the United States or no parent/legal guardian there available to provide care and physical custody. These are conjunctive status/age conditions with alternative parental-availability routes, not a definition of every foreign minor, every separated child or only orphans. The complete baseline separately defines placement as detention or an alternative; it does not decide a placement, household relationship or anyone's immigration status here.

Complete original aggravated-felony, conviction/imprisonment and crime-of-violence definitions remain bound with their own offense, sentence, amount, family and timing qualifications. They do not convert every felony into an aggravated felony. The governing Dimaya opinion addresses the 16(b) residual clause in the INA aggravated-felony context; the printed residual clause is not treated as an automatically valid classification rule. The opinion does not invalidate the entire aggravated-felony list, the distinct 16(a) elements clause or the separate child-abuse, sexual-abuse, pornography, business and prostitution predicates. No particular pending charge, conviction, background-check association or sponsor/child category is classified, and no new placement statute is adjudicated by extrapolation. These are literal qualified funding safeguards within the same House package choice, not a separate member vote or actual enforcement outcome. Other DHS and package components remain under review.

The retained USCIS operational provisions have separate permission and funding-restriction scopes. Complete section 401(a) permits otherwise available USCIS funds to acquire, operate, equip and dispose of up to five vehicles, for replacement only, in areas where the General Services Administration does not provide vehicles for lease. It is not a five-vehicle purchase mandate, permission for fleet expansion or a nationwide DHS vehicle authority. Subsection (b) permits the USCIS Director to authorize employees assigned to those areas to use those vehicles between their residences and places of employment. It does not mandate commuting use or authorize every employee in every area. No purchase, disposal, commuting authorization or actual travel is inferred.

Complete section 402 bars use of funds appropriated by this Act to process or approve a competition under OMB Circular A-76 for services provided by five named USCIS employee classes, including temporary or term employees: Immigration Information Officers, Immigration Service Analysts, Contact Representatives, Investigative Assistants and Immigration Services Officers. The restriction is tied to the Act's funds, the process/approval of that competition and those employee-provided services. It does not become a ban on all contracting, all outsourcing, every DHS employee's services or use of every possible funding source. No actual competition, contract award, job loss, citizenship qualification, immigration benefit or service delay is established.

The bound official archival A-76 text is the May 29, 2003 revised circular with its identified August 2003 technical correction and March 2008 changes, not the superseded 1999 circular. Complete material main-circular scope, transition and referenced-memoranda notes and the Competition definition remain. Competition includes formal source evaluation under stated rules, including streamlined and standard processes and specified prior-version comparisons/conversions; this procurement context is not collapsed into every purchase or contract. Unreviewed attachments, costing algorithms, referenced-memorandum applications and the law of any particular competition are not supplied here. These operational provisions concern USCIS capacity, without a predicted staffing, processing or individual status outcome.

Complete section 515 also qualifies the retained reporting architecture: an official required by this Act to report or certify to the House and Senate Appropriations Committees may not delegate authority to perform that act unless specifically authorized in the Act. The exception is retained. This does not invent a new deadline, recipient cohort, filing outcome or general prohibition on all DHS delegation; the separately bound ICE Director and CFO report actors remain distinct. Blue Campaign and other DHS/program and package components remain under review. These selected provisions remain part of one whole-package choice, not separate member positions.

The retained Blue Campaign provision is a qualified program transfer within mixed DHS funding. Complete section 542(a) says not less than $5 million made available in that Act shall be transferred to ICE Operations and Support to support and conduct necessary Blue Campaign operations for its printed fiscal year 2024. The amount is a minimum, not a $5 million ceiling or an observed transfer/spend. Subsection (b) requires notification to both House and Senate Appropriations Committees before obligation of those funds. It is not permission to notify only after spending. The printed fiscal year is preserved beside complete H.R. 1968 section 1105's general continuance through the section 1106 date; the combined fiscal-year application is reserved rather than replacing every 2024 reference with 2025 or declaring the rider automatically inoperative. No exact new-year allocation or actual notification is asserted.

The complete original 2024 Blue Campaign statute defines a DHS program headed by a Secretary-appointed Director to unify and coordinate Department efforts against human trafficking. Its guidance, training, information-sharing, public awareness, partnerships and trauma-informed victim-service coordination have broader scope than Immigration alone. Border and airport-checkpoint victim identification and aviation-worker training are among its distinct responsibilities; no border crossing, foreign citizenship, lack of lawful status or immigration benefit is required by the bound trafficking definitions. This minimum program transfer is not all ICE detention/removal funding, entirely immigration spending or a payment/immigration entitlement for every victim. No actual victim, trafficker, referral, prosecution, immigration status or service outcome is identified.

The statute's printed definition references paragraphs (9) and (10) of 22 USC 7102. Its explicit original editorial reference note identifies their redesignation to (11) and (12); the reference is preserved with that source-grounded numbering context, not silently pointed at current minimum-standards or foreign-assistance definitions. Complete severe-trafficking and sex-trafficking definitions remain distinct. Severe sex trafficking requires a commercial sex act induced by force, fraud or coercion, or a person induced to perform it under eighteen; the labor/services route requires the stated force/fraud/coercion and involuntary-servitude/peonage/debt-bondage/slavery purpose. The separate sex-trafficking definition covers the listed acts for a commercial sex act without importing every severe-form qualifier into it. Commercial act, coercion, legal-process abuse, debt-bondage and involuntary-servitude definitions remain bound in full; no individual conduct, criminal liability or victim classification is adjudicated.

Complete statutory governance and historical transfer notes retain the advisory/consultation architecture, the specified ten-year web-training period and the 2022 Blue Campaign functions/resources transfer to the Center for Countering Human Trafficking. They do not establish new H.R. 1968 transfer events, actual performance, new appropriations-committee recipients or a universal status-based program. Existing program-operation and victim-service references do not adjudicate a person's assistance entitlement. This is source-bound mixed-program context within the same whole-package choice; no separate member trafficking stance or complete package coverage is inferred. Other DHS and DOJ/State/migration/supplementary-act components remain under review.

The selected DOJ court-funding mechanism is the separately bound EOIR account in the incorporated 2024 Commerce/Justice/Science division, read with complete H.R. 1968 section 1101(a)(2) and its stated substitutions/exclusions. The EOIR account provides $844 million for necessary administration of immigration-related activities, of which $4 million is derived by transfer from EOIR fees deposited in the Immigration Examinations Fee account. The $4 million is included in, not added to, the $844 million; no $848 million total or direct fee-rate increase is inferred. Not less than $28 million within the account is available for Legal Orientation Program services and activities. That is a minimum, not a ceiling or an individual right to a lawyer, actual representation, service or legal outcome.

The same complete account permits not more than $50 million of the total for courtroom-space build-out and modifications with its printed availability through September 30, 2028. H.R. 1968 section 1101(b)-(c) defines the continued level as the appropriated amount including transfers and obligation limitations; section 1102 preserves the pertinent extent/manner, while section 1103 carries comparable multi-year/no-year availability. The original printed endpoint and comparable-period rule remain distinct; no silently invented new fixed courtroom endpoint, actual construction or obligation follows. This EOIR court account is not the entire DOJ budget, ICE detention funding or a separate choice on every funded function. Exact CJS substitutions/exclusions and other package account changes remain separate rather than uniformly applied to EOIR.

Complete CJS section 205 permits transfers of not more than five percent of an appropriation among the covered current-year DOJ appropriations, with no receiving appropriation increased by more than ten percent by such transfers except as otherwise specifically provided. Both the cap and exception remain; the two specified paragraph 1(R)/COPS paragraph(7) exclusions do not become an EOIR exemption. Such transfers are treated as reprogramming and are not available for obligation except in compliance with section 505. These are permissions/conditions, not observed movement of money or a general right to move every DOJ dollar.

Complete CJS section 505 applies its reprogramming restriction to the stated Act funds, available prior-appropriation funds and agency fee-account funds, for all eight listed kinds of change. These include creating/eliminating projects, increasing restricted work, moving staff/offices, reorganizing/renaming, contracting out/privatizing federal work, qualifying augmentation/reduction and general savings that change approved work. Its augmentation threshold is more than $500,000 or ten percent, whichever is less; the separate funding/personnel reduction trigger is ten percent. Both Appropriations Committees must be notified fifteen days in advance of the covered reprogramming. It is not every purchase, every budget change regardless of those predicates, after-the-fact notification or whichever threshold is greater. Section 209 also applies those notification thresholds/procedures to deviations from specified activity amounts in the Act/explanatory statement and use of previous-year deobligated balances. Unreviewed explanatory-statement allocations are not imported as new meaning.

The complete original fee-account deposit/reimbursement rules remain bound without changing rates, treating every fee as unrestricted, overriding territorial saving clauses or counting reimbursement as an additional appropriation. No actual fee collection, transfer, reprogramming, report, courtroom opening, case speed, representation or individual immigration status/outcome is established. These are literal qualified court-capacity and funding-control objects within the same House package choice; no distinct member position on a court, program or transfer is inferred. Remaining DOJ/State/migration/supplementary-act and other components continue under review.

The selected State Criminal Alien Assistance Program funding is the separately identified paragraph (2) of the incorporated CJS State and Local Law Enforcement Assistance account. That paragraph specifies $234 million for SCAAP under INA section 241(i)(5), with a restriction that no jurisdiction request compensation above its actual cost for Federal immigration and other detainees housed in State and local detention facilities. The account's printed no-year availability remains subject to H.R. 1968 section 1103's comparable-availability rule. Exact section 1301(4) replaces the mixed account total with $2,000,033,000, paragraph (1) with $499,033,000 and paragraph (1)(Q)/(R) with zero; it does not replace SCAAP paragraph (2)'s $234 million with the account total, $499,033,000 or zero. Excluded CJS section 222 convention funding is not SCAAP funding. These are specified budget objects, not actual net awards, a new individual benefit or a claim that the whole account is immigration funding.

Complete pre-vote INA 241(i) preserves the chief executive's written request and, as determined by the Attorney General, a contractual compensation arrangement or Federal custody/incarceration alternative. The complete definition requires a felony conviction or two or more misdemeanor convictions, together with one of the three stated status routes: entry without inspection or outside designated time/place; exclusion/deportation proceedings when taken into State/local custody; or admission as a nonimmigrant with failure to maintain the admitted/changed status or comply with its conditions when taken into that custody. It is not every noncitizen, every person without lawful status or an arrest without the stated conviction predicate. Original agency/proceedings wording is retained without silently mapping it to a modern case determination. The average State incarceration-cost basis as determined by the Attorney General and the separate appropriations actual-cost restriction remain distinct; no individual reimbursement formula or award is computed.

The baseline also retains Federal-incarceration priority for the specified aggravated-felony group, security appropriate to conviction, its printed fiscal-year 2006-2011 authorization amounts and correctional-purpose-only use of distributed funds under that authorization. Those dated authorizations are not new H.R. 1968 appropriations or a promised $750-$950 million award, and correctional purpose is not unrestricted general policing. No person's conviction/status, aggravated-felony classification, detention/removal, jurisdiction entitlement or actual custody transfer is adjudicated.

Complete CJS section 212 preserves two distinct up-to-two-percent mechanisms at the Attorney General's discretion: Office of Justice Programs training/technical assistance may use up to two percent of covered grant/reimbursement funds; up to two percent of covered funds may be transferred and merged into NIJ/BJS research, evaluation or statistics, except funds specifically appropriated for those NIJ/BJS purposes. The latter text's shall-transfer direction remains subject to the stated discretion and up-to cap, without a guaranteed actual transfer. The express paragraph (1)(R) exclusion does not become an exclusion for SCAAP paragraph (2). These are not an automatic four-percent deduction or a computed guaranteed net SCAAP award. Already-bound CJS 205/209/505 source/receiving limits, exceptions, deviation/prior-deobligation rules and qualifying advance notification still apply; no unlimited transfer or every-expenditure notice claim.

This is a qualified criminal-alien incarceration-assistance funding object within the whole House package choice. It does not create a separate member stance on an individual detainee, jurisdiction, grant or custody option. Remaining prisoner/alien transportation, trafficking victim programs, State/migration/refugee/supplementary authorities and other package components continue under review.

The selected Marshals mechanism is the incorporated Federal Prisoner Detention account and its responsibility for managing the Justice Prisoner and Alien Transportation System (JPATS), read with exact H.R. 1968 section 1302(2). That section replaces the account level with $2,236,000,000 rather than adding that amount to the original $2.1 billion. The broad account supports United States prisoners in Marshals custody; its total is not a separately allocated Immigration or JPATS transportation budget. The original account's $250 million emergency designation is within its printed total, not an additional $250 million. The complete budget baseline requires enacted discretionary-account appropriations and both a congressional account-specific emergency designation and a subsequent presidential designation for that adjustment route. No actual presidential designation, new fixed budget-cap adjustment, observed spend or silently resolved fiscal-year application is inferred.

The account permits not more than $20 million within its funds to be considered State and local law-enforcement assistance funds for 18 USC 4013(b). This is a cap, not a minimum, an additional appropriation or a $20 million actual award. Complete 4013(a)-(c) preserves clothing, medical care/guard hire and qualified housing/care/security support, its State/local/territorial contract/cooperative-agreement and guaranteed Federal-bed-space route, average per-inmate construction-cost limit, assured Federal availability, and allowable costs or other conditions specified in the contract for per-diem rates. The construction-cost limit and per-diem contractual alternative are distinct; this is not a universal actual-cost-only rule for every detention agreement. Printed private-entity conditions retain district need designation, American Correctional Association standards, applicable law, approved fire/security/escape/riot plans, other Marshals rules and an opportunity for public comment. No private facility's eligibility, contract award, regulatory compliance or individual detention is established.

The same captured statutory notes separately retain reasonable-basis/reasonable-duration detention-contract authority notwithstanding the stated other-law provisions. The published December 31, 2002 OLC opinion is bound as attributed executive legal qualification context: its complete 4013 discussion recognizes other contract conditions, including fixed-price terms not coextensive with costs. The opinion's historical (a)(4)(C) label is traced by the original Code amendment note to current (b)(3), rather than mistaken for an absent current clause. This does not waive every procurement/safety condition, resolve a modern contract dispute or convert historical agency names into new H.R. 1968 authority.

The complete current JPATS fund note covers scheduling/transportation of United States prisoners and the printed illegal/criminal-alien categories in Marshals custody, not every noncitizen or every DHS civil detainee. It retains necessary salary/operations/aircraft/support-facility expenses, reimbursement or advance-credit rates recovering operating expense including leave and depreciation, credit of aircraft-disposal proceeds, no-year fund availability and operating-equipment leases not exceeding ten years. The older five-year predecessor is not substituted for that current ten-year limit; this equipment-lease limit is not a universal duration limit for the separate reasonable-duration detention-contract authority. Management responsibility and this existing reimbursable fund are distinct from assigning the whole $2.236 billion account to transport, adding an unprinted JPATS appropriation, a removal power or actual flights, transfers, aircraft acquisition or individual classification.
