Complete CJS section 206 restricts BOP or Marshals use of the stated title funds to transport a person who is a prisoner pursuant to a State/Federal conviction and classified maximum or high security, except to an appropriately secure BOP-certified prison or other facility. Both the conviction and security predicates remain; it is not every civil immigration detainee, all DHS transport or a blanket ban on transport. Already-bound 205/209/505 transfer/deviation/reprogramming limits and advance-notice conditions, exact continuance/comparable availability and charging of earlier continuing-resolution expenditures remain. These literal funding/management objects are part of the whole House package choice; they establish no separate member position on a contract, facility, detainee or flight. Remaining trafficking victim programs, State/migration/refugee assistance, supplementary acts and exact package counterparts continue under review.

The selected trafficking victim-services funding is paragraph (3) of the incorporated CJS State and Local Law Enforcement Assistance account. It specifies $88 million for victim-services programs under three alternative named authorities: section 107(b)(2) of the printed Victims of Trafficking Act reference, the Trafficking Victims Protection Reauthorization Act of 2005, or programs authorized under Public Law 113-4. Exact H.R. 1968 section 1301(4) changes the mixed account total and paragraph (1)/(1)(Q)/(1)(R), not paragraph (3)'s $88 million. That sum is not the whole account, an additional $88 million or an allocation of the whole line to any one of the three authorities. The already-bound containing-account no-year clause remains qualified by comparable availability and continuance rules. No actual grant, net award or individual entitlement is inferred.

The first named authority is read through the complete pre-vote 22 USC 7105(b)(2) grant paragraph, within the subsection for victims in the United States. Subject to available appropriations, the Attorney General may make grants to States, Indian tribes, local government units and nonprofit nongovernmental victims' service organizations to develop, expand or strengthen human-trafficking victim-service programs. The listed trauma-informed care or housing examples are nonexclusive: victims ages 12-24 who are also homeless, in foster care or involved in the criminal justice system; victims transitioning out of foster care; or women or girls in underserved populations. The age and circumstance requirements are joined within the first example, while the three examples are alternatives. They are not a universal age floor, women-only beneficiary rule or requirement that every victim satisfy all three examples.

Of amounts made available for grants under this paragraph, the mandatory set-asides are three percent for research/evaluation/statistics, five percent for training/technical assistance including provider protection from intimidation or retaliation, and one percent for management/administration. These percentages attach to funds for grants under 7105(b)(2), not automatically to the entire $88 million line covering alternative authorities. They remain separate from CJS section 212's two qualified up-to-two-percent mechanisms and their discretion/exceptions. No fixed nine-percent or combined deduction from the whole line, guaranteed net grant amount, observed transfer or legal priority between mechanisms is calculated.

The Federal share may not exceed 75 percent of total project cost. This limits the project share, not 75 percent of the $88 million appropriation. In general, the match may use contributions or expenditures improving victim-support services and recovery/reintegration, consistent with grant requirements and approved project scope. It is not an unconditional waiver of matching or approval requirements.

The discretionary priority applies only when selecting grants available solely for law-enforcement operations or task forces. The Attorney General may prioritize an applicant attesting that funds will prevent severe trafficking, strengthen investigation/prosecution of those knowingly benefiting financially from a trafficking venture, affirmatively avoid arresting/charging/prosecuting victims for offenses directly resulting from victimization, and not condition access to shelter or restorative services on collaboration with law enforcement. The applicant must also attest to dedicated anti-trafficking law-enforcement resources extending beyond the grant's duration. These are combined attestation conditions for that discretionary priority; they are not mandatory priority for every grant, a universal prohibition for every service program or a separate promise that a particular application succeeds.

This funded grant paragraph does not establish an individual immigration status, admission, visa, certification, removal decision or benefit entitlement. Its program scope is not silently narrowed by importing separate individual-assistance/certification provisions from the broader statute. The other two named authorities still require current program mapping and material operative review; original 2005/2013 text alone is not treated as the current grant rule, an expired/unavailable authority or closure of their programs. Remaining State/migration/refugee assistance, supplementary acts, other DHS and exact package counterparts also continue under review. These qualified funding objects stay part of the whole House passage choice without a separate member stance on a victim, applicant, grant or priority determination.

The current domestic minor-victim block-grant program is shared authority context for the same trafficking paragraph (3), not another appropriation or a separate member vote. Complete pre-vote 34 USC 20702 identifies its source as 2005 Act section 202, amended by Public Law 113-4 section 1241(a) and later laws, with its former 42 USC 14044a classification traced in the original notes. The original 2005 section 202 HHS program for United States citizens or permanent residents, original 75-percent project share and 2006-2007 authorization are historical, not imported as current recipient or matching rules. The original 2013 four-year sunset is also historical: current notes preserve the 2018 restoration of the March 6, 2017 text with retroactive effect as though enacted on that date and repeal of the sunset provision. This candidate does not declare the program expired from the 2013 clause or a new H.R. 1968 program from that restoration.

The current definition covers a person younger than 18 who is a victim of an offense described in 18 USC 1591(a) or comparable State law, or a person ages 18-20 who met the under-18 definition before turning 18 and was receiving shelter or services as a minor victim. It is not every 18-20-year-old, every trafficking victim or a citizenship/permanent-residence eligibility rule. Complete 1591(a), its qualified age-knowledge exception and all definitions remain source-bound: knowingly described recruitment/transport/provision/advertising/maintenance/patronizing/soliciting acts with the stated commerce/jurisdiction predicate, or the benefiting-from-a-venture alternative, retain the knowledge or qualified reckless-disregard condition. That reckless-disregard route excludes a paragraph (1) advertising violation. Force/fraud/coercion or the under-18 commercial-sex branch are alternatives, with the printed condition that the person will be caused to engage in a commercial sex act; force is not required for every under-18 case. The reasonable-opportunity-to-observe exception is limited to the stated (a)(1) prosecution and listed acts and removes proof of under-age knowledge/recklessness, not every offense element. Commercial sex, venture participation, serious harm, coercion and abuse of legal process retain their complete definitions. No actual offense, State-law equivalence, conviction, sentence or person's victim status is adjudicated.

The Assistant Attorney General, consulting the HHS Assistant Secretary for Children and Families, may make block grants to four eligible State/local entities in different United States regions, with at least one in a State population below five million. The block-grant provisions specify a $1.5-$2 million range subject to available appropriations under the printed subsection (g) reference, plus a one-year term and up to three discretionary one-year renewals. Subsection (g) contains matching requirements while subsection (i) contains authorization of appropriations. The application of that printed amount condition is reserved for bounded review; it is not silently redirected to (i), converted to an unconditional current award or used to allocate the whole line; in later fiscal-year grantmaking, preceding-year recipients eligible for renewal receive mandatory priority, taking available evaluations into account. These are program grant objects, not four guaranteed observed awards, an extra $6-$8 million appropriation or allocation of the entire $88 million line. Eligible entities retain significant minor-sex-trafficking activity, demonstrated interagency/provider cooperation, the complete multidisciplinary care/training/prevention/referral/screening plan and assurance that funded residential care or services will not require a minor victim's law-enforcement collaboration. Qualified nongovernmental providers must have demonstrated relevant service experience or specialized staff, together with a sustainability plan; the two expertise alternatives are not both mandatory.

At least 67 percent of each block grant must be used for the specified residential care and services through qualified nongovernmental organizations, as described in the four care-use clauses: residential care, round-the-clock emergency services, clothing/daily necessities and case management. This does not declare that each victim must receive all four services. This is a minimum within each grant, not all activities or the whole $88 million line. The complete other permitted uses retain counseling/substance treatment, legal services, specialized training, outreach/education and minor severe-trafficking screening/referral. Treatment of people charged or cited with purchasing sex is limited to the stated sentence/prosecution-alternative setting and excludes a person charged with purchasing sex with a minor. It does not authorize treatment of every purchaser or erase criminal charges. Application assurances, annual contracted evaluation and consultation to avoid unintentional duplication remain, without an actual agency-compliance finding.

The separate 2023 pilot within current subsection (b)(5) must be established by the Assistant Attorney General consulting the Assistant Secretary. Community organizations in underserved communities, prioritizing rural communities, may apply for housing-unit-based replicable treatment/support models. Its primarily adolescent/youth recipient alternatives include transitioning from foster care, substance-use disorder, pregnancy/parenting and the listed foster/child-welfare, poverty, abuse/neglect, trafficking, juvenile-justice, gang or homelessness histories. This pilot is not confined to the block grant's defined minor sex-trafficking-victim cohort or a guarantee that every listed person receives services. Its complete eight permitted uses and mandatory funding priority for the described crisis/shelter/addiction and transitional-age residential programs remain distinct, without assigning a fixed share of the $88 million or declaring actual establishment or awards.

Current safeguards preserve the two-fiscal-year exclusion following the year an unauthorized expenditure or unallowable cost is reported, the five-prior-fiscal-year Government-grant compliance bar, and the three-percent administration cap on the total amount appropriated to carry out this section. The non-Federal match minima are 15/25/40/50 percent of the grant in the first year and successive renewal periods; these are not the historical 75-percent Federal project-cost ceiling or the first authority's distinct grant-share rule. Printed 2016/2017 Inspector General audits, fiscal-year 2018-2021 $8 million authorizations and thirty-month-after-March-7-2013 GAO report remain dated provisions, not new current appropriations, automatic program termination or observed completion. Applying for section 20705 grants does not prevent also applying here; that savings clause is not acceptance of every other program's qualifications. CJS transfer/continuance/section 212 conditions remain separately qualified, with no computed net grant or combined automatic deduction.

This adds one current shared program meaning despite its appearance under both named act authorities, preserving qualified services and grants without individual immigration permission, certification or benefit entitlement. Other current 2005/2013 trafficking programs and their material references remain executable research, including the distinct rewritten child-trafficking program and section 20705. State/migration/refugee assistance, supplementary acts, other DHS, exact counterparts and final whole-package comparison also remain open. No whole-authority or package closure, independent acceptance or separate member stance on an applicant, victim, provider or program choice.

The selected additional-special-assessment amendment is exact H.R. 1968 division C section 3103, which would replace March 14, 2025 with September 30, 2025 in 18 USC 3014. The complete pre-vote assessment provision and explicit enactment-date note retain the May 29, 2015 starting reference. This changes the printed assessment-authority ending date, not the $5,000 amount, the separate section 3013 assessment, every offense/conviction date, all Federal fines or the duration of an already imposed payment obligation. It is a direct section 3103 change, not inferred from the general appropriation continuance. No actual enactment, court assessment or collection is asserted.

The unchanged $5,000 assessment requires a non-indigent person or entity convicted under one of five named branches: the peonage/slavery/trafficking chapter, sexual-abuse chapter, child sexual-exploitation/abuse chapter, transportation-for-illegal-sexual-activity chapter, or INA section 274. It is not every person with an immigration violation, every noncitizen, an arrest/allegation without conviction or every trafficking victim. The INA 274 branch retains the complete printed family-only entry exception, with the stated spouse/parent/son/daughter relationship at the time of action and no other individual; it is not a broad family shield for any offense or all assistance, and its printed referent is not silently reassigned to decide a case. The larger mixed criminal-offense list is not treated wholly as Immigration funding or a separate member stance on each crime.

Complete INA 274 criminal subsection (a) is bound as the named conviction context. Its distinct bringing/transporting/harboring/encouraging/conspiracy/assistance, bringing-without-prior-authorization, knowing-ten-hires-in-twelve-months and aggravated commercial/group-danger branches retain their own knowledge, conduct and penalty qualifications. The qualified religious-denomination/nonprofit volunteer-minister exception remains distinct, including its limits on encouraging entry; it is not an exemption for all religious activity. The already-bound unauthorized-alien definition is employment-specific at the particular time, retaining lawful permanent residence or statutory/Attorney-General employment authorization alternatives. No all-noncitizen employment rule, new criminal offense, unrestricted reading of encouragement, modern speech/prosecution holding, actual charge/conviction/sentence or person's status is established by extending the assessment date.

The assessment is not payable until all outstanding court-ordered fines, restitution and other victim-compensation obligations from its underlying convictions have been satisfied. The collection method remains the criminal-fine method subject to that priority, including civil remedies authorized by section 3613 where appropriate; this is not immediate assessment collection before restitution or blanket seizure of every asset. Section 3014(g)'s pay-until-full language remains subject to complete 3613(b). Fine liability terminates at the later of twenty years from entry of judgment or twenty years after release from imprisonment; it also terminates upon the individual's death. Restitution liability terminates at the later of twenty years from entry of judgment or twenty years after release from imprisonment. On death, the individual's estate is responsible for any unpaid restitution balance; the subsection (c) lien continues until the estate receives written release of that liability. No universal perpetual assessment, September-30 discharge of existing liability or claim that death cancels every restitution debt. No individual balance, indigence finding, deadline, property/lien eligibility or estate release is calculated.

The named Domestic Trafficking Victims' Fund is an existing Treasury fund administered by the Attorney General consulting DHS and HHS. Its transfer is an amount equal to assessments collected, available until expended, not every nominal charge as an observed receipt or a new fixed appropriation. Complete Treasury deposit text preserves the printed section 3718(b) exception; its explicit original reference note identifies the redesignation to current 3718(d). Complete material current 3718 keeps qualified agency/private-counsel contracts, retained dispute/claim/termination authority and applicable privacy/debt-collection conditions. A qualifying contract under (a) or (b) may pay a recovery fee from recovered amounts; the appropriation-effectiveness limit has its express fee-contract exception, and this section excludes Internal Revenue Code debts. No actual contract/fee or unconditional zero-fee/no-exception net-deposit calculation is inferred. This fund and its collected-assessment mechanism are separate from assigning the whole CJS $88 million line to Immigration, child grants or a guaranteed net award. Its other use/health-transfer clauses and their material authorities, including the separate H.R. 1968 health-funding conforming amendment, remain under review. This bounded date/assessment/collection review does not close the whole fund, chapter-crime universe, child-trafficking program, other acts or whole package.

The whole House passage choice includes this qualified amendment; no separate member vote on an offender, victim, family relationship, agency transfer or medical service is inferred. Remaining current child-trafficking and State/local programs, State/migration/refugee assistance, supplementary acts, other DHS, exact counterparts and final package comparison continue as executable research. Prior application questions remain separate and unchanged.

The distinct current child-trafficking deterrence block-grant program is another qualified use of the same trafficking paragraph (3), not a separate appropriation or member vote. Complete pre-vote 34 USC 20703 traces to 2005 Act section 203, formerly 42 USC 14044b, and records the 2015 general rewrite. The complete original 2005 HHS residential-treatment pilot is historical: its citizenship/permanent-residence and under-18-at-identification cohort, three sites, establishment/report deadlines and old authorization are not current 20703 rules. Current Attorney General block grants may support eligible State/local programs; the current child definition is under 18 and the severe-trafficking predicate is reused from complete current 7102 definitions, including sex-trafficking and forced-labor branches. It is not only sex trafficking, every child, a citizenship/LPR condition or the separate 20702 qualified ages 18-20 continuation.

Eligible State/local entities retain significant child-trafficking criminal activity, demonstrated Federal/State/local and applicable tribal cooperation, and the complete workable multidisciplinary plan. That plan includes shelter, trauma-informed gender-responsive care, training, prevention/deterrence/prosecution, runaway/homeless-youth referrals, screening all prostitution arrestees whether adult or child for trafficking and other victimization, and child-welfare/advocacy-center cooperation. The printed prosecution phrase remains source-bound without silently repairing its wording. A child victim's access to funded shelter or services must not require law-enforcement collaboration. Witness programs and court activities may encourage cooperation; encouragement does not erase that access assurance. No grant funds may be awarded or transferred to an entity unless it has substantial relevant service experience or specialized staff; those are alternatives, not two cumulative qualifications or automatic eligibility for every provider.

Complete permitted activities retain specialized training including State safe-harbor laws, dedicated task forces and investigation expenses, prosecution units, victim/witness safety and relocation, other victim assistance and finding homeless/runaway youth including retired Federal officers. Officer salary funding cannot exceed the percentage of on-duty time devoted to child-trafficking cases; prosecutor salary funding cannot exceed the percentage of total worked hours devoted to those cases. These are distinct time-based caps, not full salary entitlement or a fixed share of the whole $88 million line.

The problem-solving-court branch preserves mandatory regular judicial training, continuing supervision of a potential child victim identified by a law-enforcement or judicial officer whether charged or not, individualized court-ordered treatment, consolidated case management and regular mandatory victim appearances. Its ultimate dismissal is limited to relevant nonviolent charges following successful compliance with the court-ordered program. It does not dismiss all charges automatically, eliminate appearances or identify every participant as an adjudicated trafficking victim. The seven treatment categories and coordinated services remain qualified permitted activities, without an individual treatment, criminal-case or cooperation judgment.

Applications must describe activities and a detailed fund-use plan, supply required assurances, and disclose pending similar Federal grant applications plus similar grants received during the preceding five years. The Attorney General must prefer a plan covering all activities in subsection (b)(1)-(3) or a plan continuing all award-funded activities after the award expires. Those are alternative routes to preference, not both required, a guarantee of award or a requirement that every applicant propose every court activity. Recently beginning to solicit child-trafficking data must not disadvantage an otherwise eligible entity. A grant expires three years after award and may renew no more than twice, each renewal lasting no more than two years; these are not the separate minor-victim program's one-year and three-renewal terms.

Periodic nongovernmental evaluations, Inspector General review of methodological/statistical validity and reporting results to both Judiciary Committees remain mandatory agency duties, without an observed completion finding. Unauthorized-cost exclusion lasts two fiscal years following the reported year; the separate compliance bar examines the five fiscal years before application. Administration is capped at five percent of total amount expended to carry out this section. The Federal program-cost share is 70/60/50 percent in the first, second and third-or-later years. These are expenditure-based administration and program-cost Federal shares, not the other program's three-percent appropriated-amount cap, 15/25/40/50 grant match or the first authority's 75-percent project-cost ceiling. They do not create an automatic combined deduction or computed net award.

The printed fund authorization permits the Attorney General, consulting HHS, to award no more than $7 million from available Domestic Trafficking Victims' Fund money for each fiscal year 2016-2020. The previously bound complete 3014 fund-identity/collected-amount provisions are reused. This dated authorization is not a new H.R. 1968 $7 million appropriation, the whole $88 million allocation, automatic expiration of the program or an actual observed award. Material fund-use/health-transfer clauses, their conditions and the separate exact 2101(d)-(e) health conforming edit remain executable research; this increment does not close the fund or compute current available money.

The child-advocacy-center definition retains the printed 42 USC 13001 et seq. reference and its explicit original note tracing reclassification to 34 USC 20301 et seq. Material current center context preserves physical/sexual abuse or neglect including human trafficking and child pornography, coordinated multidisciplinary response, and nonoffending family excluding a member convicted or accused of child abuse. The local-center site criterion identifies an appropriate investigation/treatment/counseling site for child victims and nonoffending family. Its introduction says grant criteria may require listed elements; the written interagency agreement and site are not silently made universal conditions for every 20703 entity. This is center-reference context, not proof that a particular center was created under the Act, a new center grant or completion of all center eligibility, administration and funding authorities. Those further authorities remain research where materially applied.

All uses remain components of the whole H.R. 1968 passage choice, projected once for both members. Current 20705 and material fund/medical-transfer authorities, State/migration/refugee assistance, supplementary acts, other DHS, exact counterparts and final whole-package comparison remain open. No individual immigration permission, victim/provider eligibility or criminal disposition, new application question, whole-authority closure or editorial acceptance follows from this candidate increment.

The current State/local trafficking law-enforcement grant program is another qualified authority component of the same CJS trafficking line, not a separate member vote or whole-line allocation. Complete pre-vote 34 USC 20705 maps to original 2005 section 204, formerly 42 USC 14044c. Complete original section 204 and 2013 section 1242 preserve the actual citizenship/permanent-residence condition and its express deletion; that old condition is not a current recipient or offense limitation. The territorial-jurisdiction requirement remains: the described severe-trafficking acts and related offenses occur wholly or partly within the United States. Related offenses include tax, illegal-proceeds, money-laundering, racketeering and other criminal violations committed in connection with sex trafficking or a severe form of trafficking. This is not every unrelated tax or financial offense, every offense worldwide or an individual immigration/criminal classification.

The Attorney General may make grants to States and local law-enforcement agencies for the complete listed program purposes: investigation/prosecution, victim-identification training, purchaser investigations/prosecutions prioritizing minor-victim cases, education of persons charged with or convicted of purchasing or attempting to purchase commercial sex, trust/cooperation training, and as appropriate designation of at least one severe-trafficking prosecutor. These are qualified grant purposes, not a new criminal offense, actual prosecution, universal prosecutor appointment, automatic award or proof that every grantee performs every purpose. The purchaser-case priority does not restrict all grant purposes to child cases. The printed severe-trafficking reference to 7102(9) retains its explicit original note tracing redesignation to current 7102(11); existing complete current definitions are reused without silent reference repair or a separate individual victim determination.

Grants may be made only for programs where the State/local law-enforcement agency collaborates with social-service providers and relevant nongovernmental organizations, including organizations experienced in services to trafficked persons. That mandatory program collaboration is distinct from training officers to encourage a person's cooperation with prosecution. It does not itself require every victim to collaborate with police, turn the nonexclusive experienced-organization example into the only possible partner, or import the separate 20702/20703 service-access assurances as new 20705 text. The current Federal share cannot exceed 75 percent of the total costs of projects described in the application. This is a Federal project-cost ceiling, not a minimum, a percent of the entire $88 million, the other program's grant match or the child program's year-based Federal shares. Existing qualified CJS transfer, research/evaluation and notification rules remain separately bound; no automatic combined deduction, invented program administration cap or net award is calculated.

An entity applying for a 20702 grant is not prohibited from also applying here; current 20702 separately preserves the reciprocal savings. Concurrent applications do not guarantee eligibility, awards, double funding or both programs' conditions being interchangeable. Current authorization is $10 million for each fiscal year 2014-2021, distinct from original 2005 $25 million for fiscal years 2006-2007 and the 2013 amendment's then-2014-2017 range. Those dated authorization objects are not new H.R. 1968 appropriations, observed grants or automatic termination of the program. The GAO study/report duty within thirty months after March 7, 2013 and its specified evaluation/recommendation scope remains dated, without claiming the report occurred or imposing a new current deadline.

This completes the bounded current 20705 program and identified original/current mapping, not all trafficking-fund applications or the whole package. Material fund-use/medical-transfer conditions and exact 2101(d)-(e), further center authorities where applied, State/migration/refugee assistance, supplementary acts, other DHS, exact counterparts and final package comparison remain executable research. No new application question, individual status/benefit/provider/criminal disposition, separate member stance or editorial acceptance is inferred.

The separately printed citizen/permanent-resident trafficking-assistance program remains a qualified authority context for the fund, not the current 20705 program whose old citizenship condition was deleted. Complete current 7105(f)(1)-(3) directs HHS and the Attorney General, consulting Labor, to establish assistance for United States citizens or aliens lawfully admitted for permanent residence who are victims of severe trafficking. Both the status alternative and severe-victim predicate remain; this is not every citizen/resident, every noncitizen, only child sex trafficking or a new immigration-status grant. Existing complete 1101(a)(20) defines lawful permanent residence as the lawfully accorded privilege of residing permanently in the United States as an immigrant under immigration laws, such status not having changed. Existing complete severe-trafficking definitions are reused. No actual citizenship/permanent-residence/victim status, certification, admission or adjustment determination is made.

The two agencies must consult victim-service nongovernmental organizations about the most beneficial assistance. Alongside specialized services, the program must facilitate provider communication/coordination, identification of providers and referrals to programs for which victims are already eligible, including DOJ/HHS programs. Referral to existing eligible programs is not a new entitlement or blanket eligibility for every Federal benefit. The exact H.R.22 EH proposal adds documentary proof of United States citizenship to covered NVRA federal voter-registration applications, including motor-vehicle, mail and designated-agency routes. The proposed definition accepts: a REAL ID-consistent identification that indicates U.S. citizenship; a valid U.S. passport; military ID together with a service record showing U.S. birth; valid Federal/State/Tribal photo ID showing U.S. birth; or other valid such photo ID together with specified certified birth, contemporaneous hospital-birth, adoption, consular-birth, naturalization/citizenship/other INA-issued proof, or DHS American Indian Card with KIC classification. The birth-certificate route has seven printed content/issuance/file/signature/seal requirements. Not every REAL ID, military ID, Tribal ID or American Indian card alone qualifies. Mail applicants must present proof in person by the State application deadline, or at a permitted same-day/early-voting polling place no later than election day, with notice/instructions and reasonable disability accommodations. Each State subject to the new provisions must establish an alternative process for an applicant without the listed documentary proof: signed citizenship/eligibility attestation under perjury plus other evidence and a State/local official determination, accompanied by the official's affidavit using EAC minimum standards/basis. A separate discrepancy-documentation process is required. The bill does not eliminate these alternatives or itself decide a particular document/name/status case. Covered States must take ongoing citizenship-check steps and establish the specified verification program within 30 days. State-requested necessary citizenship-verification information, including requested batches, must be supplied by a Federal agency head possessing it within 24 hours without a fee; Federal agencies share information to respond, and the specified sources include existing DHS SAVE, SSA verification, State-ID and other confirmation databases. The bill also directs DHS to investigate whether to initiate INA 239 removal proceedings if an INA-defined alien is determined through the specified information routes to be unlawfully federally registered. This is an investigation-to-determine duty, not automatic commencement or an actual removal order. States must remove confirmed noncitizens from federal voter rolls on documentation/verified information, with the proposed citizenship-ground exception to the existing 90-day systematic-roll-removal deadline; removing a voter record is not deportation. Existing INA unlawful-voting grounds concern actual unlawful voting with their own conditions and parent/residence/reasonable-belief exceptions; they do not turn registration alone into universal removability. INA 237 also retains its admitted-person framework. The INA alien definition excludes U.S. citizens and nationals; a noncitizen U.S. national is not automatically an alien. Section 5 additionally requires prompt DHS naturalization notice to the chief election official where the individual is domiciled. NVRA attestation/citizenship eligibility and the qualified 18 USC 611 alien-voting prohibition already exist; the proposal adds proof/verification and related duties rather than first banning every noncitizen vote. General passport issuance includes persons owing U.S. allegiance whether citizens or not; the bill's valid-passport proof route is preserved as printed without asserting that every passport holder is a citizen or creating citizenship. Existing SAVE is a benefit/status-verification system with privacy protections and a statutory prohibition on administrative noncriminal immigration-enforcement use. H.R.22 references that existing system and adds the investigation duty but does not expressly repeal the prohibition; their legal interaction and individual data-use/enforcement outcomes are preserved for review rather than silently resolved as a blanket repeal. The bill adds an express missing-proof-registration violation to NVRA civil notice/enforcement remedies and inserts material assistance by an executive employee to a noncitizen, or missing-proof registration, into the existing criminal provision. Its knowingly-and-willfully depriving/defrauding-election-process chapeau and maximum 5-year/fine-or-both framework are retained, not strict liability for every paperwork error. Existing private notice/cure rules remain 90 days,20 days for violations within 120 days of a federal election, and no prior notice for violations within 30 days. It adds limited criminal/immigration-proceeding exceptions to registration-office confidentiality, with the printed knowledge wording differing between motor-vehicle and Federal-mail clauses. EAC guidance is due within 10 days; voter-material changes are exempted from the Paperwork Reduction Act. Proposed applicability preserves the no-registration State exemption and printed special same-day-registration-State provisions, which refer to NVRA 8(i)/(j), not silently substituted 8(j)/(k). The bill's SAVE-use subparagraph refers to requests under paragraph(1), while the express request provision appears in(5)(A); this printed cross-reference is disclosed rather than silently repaired. Provisional-ballot ability/counting is preserved for individuals verified as citizens under new 8(j), and exemptions from non-NVRA Federal law are unaffected. The proposal takes effect on enactment and applies to applications submitted on/after that date. The whole House passage choice covers this complete scheme and its election/immigration interactions; no individual citizenship determination, registration denial, voter purge, offense, removal, effect on participation or enactment is inferred.

The complete H.R.36 EH is a Georgia foreign-policy, reporting, assistance and sanctions package. Its operative section6 adds two conditional immigration-sanctions routes, independently of the nonbinding findings/policy language. Under6(b), within 90 days of enactment the President must determine whether the specified foreign persons knowingly engaged in significant corruption or violence/intimidation in relation to blocking Georgia Euro-Atlantic integration. The covered groups are people who served in Parliament on/after January 1, 2014 or current/former senior Georgian-party officials; people currently serving in Government leadership, including law-enforcement, intelligence, judicial and local/municipal leadership; and the defined immediate family members who benefitted from the specified officials/persons conduct. An affirmative decision requires6(d)(2) sanctions; it is not a designation of every Georgian official or relative. The Secretary of State must brief within 90 days with persons and specific supporting facts. A6(b) case waiver requires the President to determine and report national-security interests or sufficiently changed circumstances; the bill states no 180-day maximum for that route. Under6(c), presidential determinations on/after enactment cover responsibility, complicity, direct/indirect engagement or attempts in actions/policies intended to undermine Georgia peace, security, stability, sovereignty or territorial integrity; leaders/officials of entities whose organization or members engaged in those activities; and the defined benefitting immediate family members of sanctioned persons. This route permits property blocking and requires the immigration sanction, plus briefing/written notice within 10 days of imposition. Its separate waiver is renewable for no more than 180 days per period, with national-security determination and written justification submitted at least 15 days before effectiveness. Section6(d)(2) makes a qualifying foreign person THAT IS AN INA ALIEN inadmissible, ineligible for visa/entry documentation, admission, parole and any other INA benefit; revocation of visa/entry documents regardless of issuance date takes immediate effect and cancels other valid entry documents. Foreign person excludes the bill-defined U.S. person: citizens, lawful permanent residents, U.S.-organized entities including foreign branches, and ANY person within the United States. INA alien excludes citizens and U.S. nationals; admission and parole remain distinct. Knowingly includes actual knowledge or should-have-known. The bill defines immediate family by EXPRESS INA201(b)(2)(A)(i) but prints the different8 USC1201 citation. The named INA provision is8 USC1151 and defines immediate relatives of U.S. CITIZENS (children, spouses, parents with citizen aged 21 or older), with qualified surviving-spouse/child and abuse-self-petition retention. This is not the simple spouse/parent/sibling/adult-child list in H.R.23. The citizenship framework and foreign-person exclusion create an application question preserved for review; the candidate does not silently repair the citation or select individuals. The bill also preserves authorized/reportable U.S. intelligence exceptions; an international-obligation exception where admission OR parole is necessary; and qualified agricultural/food/medicine/device/humanitarian transactions and related activity, including the printed6(i)(2)(C)(ii) reference to paragraph(1), not an invented universal actor exemption. No importation-of-goods sanctions authority is added. Existing IEEPA powers, exceptions and other designation authority are not made novel by the package. Section6(g) requires a broader determination and180-day report for POTENTIAL existing-IEEPA sanctions, not a second mandatory visa designation for all corruption. Necessary rules are due within 120 days with 10-day advance congressional notice. Section6(h) terminates a person sanction at certification of ceased conduct or the printed sunset reference to section7; section7 actually concerns conditional additional assistance/contacts/cooperation, with should-language, whereas section8 states the ACT ceases effect five years after enactment. Both literal provisions and the mismatched reference are retained for review, not treated as a new perpetual power or an accepted correction. Reports/assistance and other package purposes remain part of this suspension-and-passage vote. No actual corrupt conduct, sanctioned status, denial, removal, spending outcome or enactment is inferred.

The complete H.R.1503 EH combines international policy, human-rights reporting, passport authority and a mandatory sanctions-list scheme. Section4 permits, rather than requires, the Secretary of State to refuse a passport or revoke a previously issued passport only for an individual convicted under42 USC274e, still subject to imprisonment, parole or other supervised release from that conviction, who used a passport OR crossed an international border in committing that offense. Existing274e concerns knowing acquisition/receipt/transfer of a human organ for valuable consideration for human transplantation affecting interstate commerce, with the qualified paired-donation exception and exclusions for reasonable medical/handling expenses and donor travel/housing/lost wages. That predicate is not synonymous with every coercive harvesting allegation; conviction, continuing sentence/supervision and travel/document nexus are conjunctive. Its existing criminal punishment is not newly enacted here. Existing22 USC211a gives State passport-issuance authority under prescribed rules and country-use restrictions with exceptions, while212 permits passports to persons owing U.S. allegiance, including eligible nationals. The new express qualified authority is not a finding that State previously lacked every denial/revocation power. Section5 adds forced-organ-harvesting/organ-trafficking assessments to existing2151n(d) and2304(b) human-rights reports, not a wholly new reporting institution: existing State reporting has its own country scope, February 25 annual duty in2151n(d), and fiscal-year security-assistance presentation in2304(b). The bill prints an assessment in EACH foreign country, and its definitions/treatment of two subsection (i) labels are preserved rather than narrowed by inherited report headings. Section6 requires the President within 180 days of enactment to send the named congressional committees a list of each person presidentially determined to fund, sponsor or otherwise facilitate the defined forced harvesting or trafficking. That list predicate does not require the passport provision conviction. Person includes individuals, entities and the cited non-state actors: nonsovereign entities with significant political power/territorial control outside sovereign-government control, often using violence. Forced harvesting means organ removal through coercion, abduction, deception, fraud or abuse of power/vulnerability. Trafficking means recruitment, transport, transfer, harboring or receipt for organ removal by those means or controller payments/benefits. Organ incorporates274e(c)(1), including the listed human/fetal organ categories and Secretary-added organs. Listed persons face mandatory property blocking under IEEPA, without1701 emergency-declaration prerequisites. Section6(b)(2) is HEADED aliens, but its operative body says IN THE CASE OF AN INDIVIDUAL: inadmissibility, no visa/entry documentation, no admission/parole/other INA benefit, and immediate revocation regardless of issuance date cancelling other valid documents. The bill supplies no foreign-person exclusion or blanket U.S.-person principal exemption. Its separate U.S.-person definition (citizen/LPR/U.S. entity including foreign branch) describes property possession/control, not who can be listed. The candidate preserves heading/body and INA-alien/national framework without claiming citizens lose citizenship/entry rights or deciding individual applicability. No family sanction is stated. Necessary admission to comply with the UN headquarters, Vienna consular or other treaty/international agreement is excepted. Humanitarian sale/assistance/finance/transport transactions are excepted with their printed scope; no universal humanitarian immunity for every person or unrelated activity is inferred. No importation-of-goods sanctions authority is added. The President may waive sanctions/restrictions case by case for periods at most 180 days each, certifying VITAL national-security interests at least 15 days before effectiveness. Existing IEEPA implementation/penalty framework remains source-qualified, with criminal willfulness and conviction distinct from listing and civil enforcement. This whole-bill suspension-and-passage episode does not establish a component preference, actual forced harvesting, criminal conviction, designation, passport loss, immigration removal or enactment.

This May22 House passage is the whole H.R.1 reconciliation package, not a separate immigration-only vote. The controlling House choice uses H.Res.436: Rules Committee Print119-3 modified by the amendment printed in H.Rept.119-113 was considered adopted. The currently served EH incorporates later corrections and renumbering and is a comparison witness for these unchanged selected clauses, not the controlling entire vote-time text. The description selects border infrastructure, detention, State reimbursement and asylum-fee mechanisms; it does not inventory every immigration-related tax, benefit, employment-authorization, child-sponsor or removal provision in this multi-domain package. Section60001 would make additional fiscal2025 CBP appropriations available until September30,2029: $46.5billion for primary/waterborne/secondary barriers, access roads and associated detection attributes; a separate $50million for specified invasive plants impeding RioGrande border operations; and $5billion for CBP facilities/checkpoints near the southwest, northern and maritime borders. These are different purposes, not one immigration-enforcement account or actual expenditures. The adopted manager amendment adds section60004: $12billion in additional fiscal2025 DHS funds, available until September30,2029, for grants reimbursing States for costs of actions on or after January21,2021 assisting federal border/immigration enforcement, including detention/removal and combating unlawful entry of persons/contraband. Applications need satisfactory cost evidence, and DHS cannot reimburse a State already reimbursed under another DHS grant program. This is funding subject to a process and conditions, not proof of State awards or a newly conferred State removal power. Section70101 would appropriate an additional $45billion for fiscal2025 to ICE, available until September30,2029, solely for single-adult alien detention and family residential-center capacity. DHS MAY detain family units pending a removal decision and, if ordered removed, until removal. Its family-center definition includes accompanied alien children, excludes unaccompanied alien children, and expressly applies regardless of State/local facility licensing. Its single-adult detention standards clause says they shall be set in the Secretary's SOLE discretion. Preserve that printed language without importing the Senate's express consistent-with-applicable-law qualification or deciding its interaction with judicial/other legal constraints. The existing unaccompanied-child definition in6USC279(g)(2) requires no lawful immigration status, age under18, and no US parent/legal guardian or none available for care/physical custody; childhood alone does not establish that category. Capacity funding and permission are not a universal detention mandate, removal order or actual detention outcome. The relocation deadline is 120 days after the public determination, not after enactment. If the office has not moved by that deadline, its head must provide a written explanation within 5 days; operations cease from the next day until relocation, and employees are assigned to another covered office in the same State outside a defined sanctuary jurisdiction if one exists, otherwise to another such office. The Administrator must immediately remove the office head if the explanation is absent or the reasons are determined insufficient. The Administrator also cannot establish a covered office in a defined sanctuary jurisdiction. Covered office includes regional/district/local offices other than headquarters, or other fully congressionally funded SBA components under the printed definition. Existing 15 USC 633(a) already allows branch/regional offices at locations determined by the Administrator. SBA announced a six-regional-office relocation policy in March 2025; this proposal adds statutory definitions, triggers, deadlines and noncompliance consequences rather than first creating all relocation authority or proving the announced moves occurred. Existing INA custody/officer authorities, read with enacted 119-1 custody amendments, remain qualified; the bill does not independently make every detainer lawful or compel every local officer to act. H.Res.458 supplies a deemed modified pending-bill substitute and later separate final-passage context; the exact EH text controls this passage, not the earlier committee version. Actual office closures/moves, staff transfers, head removal, local wrongdoing, detention/removal, service loss or enactment is not inferred.

The exact H.R.2966 EH proposal requires the SBA Administrator to ensure every application for a loan under Small Business Act 7(a) or Small Business Investment Act titleV includes individual-applicant/individual-owner dates of birth, specified citizenship/status and ownership certifications, a certification that no direct/indirect applicant-concern owner is an ineligible person, and alien-registration numbers for LPR individual applicants or owners. The positive certification is that an individual applicant is a U.S. citizen, U.S. national or LPR, or that an applicant concern or loan guarantor is 100 percent beneficially owned by individuals in those categories. The printed ineligible-person categories are an asylee, refugee, individual issued a visa to remain in the United States, nonimmigrant under any INA 101(a)(15) subparagraph, DACA deferred-action recipient, or alien present without lawful status under the defined immigration laws. Direct/indirect ownership, not merely controlling ownership, matters. Section 2(b) makes the applicant ineligible if a post-enactment submitted application lacks required information, or if the applicant concern has any direct/indirect ineligible owner, or the individual applicant is an ineligible person. The post-enactment submission condition is printed in the missing-information route; it is not an express universal grandfathering clause for the separate status routes or proof of cancellation of existing loans. Existing 7(a) and titleV loan authorities remain, including development-company financing; the bill does not create the loan programs or guarantee approval to every positively certified person. The effective June 1,2025 SBA SOP already limits 7(a)/504 financing to 100 percent qualifying direct/indirect owners and required guarantors, with citizenship/national/LPR status, residence/entity conditions, ineligible categories, verification and its own qualified divestment/limited-guaranty exceptions. The proposal supplies statutory requirements substantially overlapping those agency restrictions, not the first restriction on noncitizen-owned borrowing. It does not expressly reproduce every SOP lookback, residence, conditional-card or limited-guaranty provision; existing program requirements are not assumed repealed, nor are agency exceptions silently inserted into the bill's text. U.S. nationality and lawful permanent residence have distinct retained INA definitions. The bill's visa/asylee/refugee labels and positive LPR certification are preserved without adjudicating an individual's prior or adjusted status. No removal of immigration status, actual application denial, loan cancellation, benefit loss or enactment is established by this House passage choice. H.Res.458's pending substitute and separate passage boundary are retained; this is the whole exact EH bill, not a component vote.

The exact H.R.884 EH proposal prohibits any individual who is not a citizen of the United States from voting in an election for public office in the District of Columbia or in any D.C. ballot initiative or referendum. Its printed criterion is citizenship, not only unlawful presence or a particular visa/LPR category; noncitizen U.S. nationals are not converted into citizens by that terminology. The proposal also repeals the entire Local Resident Voting Rights Amendment Act of 2022, D.C.Law 24-242, and restores/revives each provision it amended or repealed as if that Act had not been enacted. The local Act created an exception to the qualified-elector citizenship requirement for local elections, not federal voting. Its definition of local election covers Mayor, Council chairman/members, Attorney General, State Board of Education and Advisory Neighborhood Commissioner, plus initiative, referendum, recall and charter-amendment measures. It also changed the no-other-voting-residence/right language from State/territory to State/territory/country, removed a citizenship-statement phrase from the specified registration lead-in, and replaced citizens with residents in the specified registration provision. Those statutory modifications are part of the repeal/restoration, not silently omitted as if the bill only changed one sentence. Other voter qualifications are not replaced with unrestricted eligibility for citizens, and the bill does not repeal the entire D.C.Election Code or every later election amendment. The local Act's effective/congressional-review provisions and budget-inclusion applicability condition are retained as baseline; the candidate makes no independent claim that a particular person was registered or voted under it. Existing 18 USC 611 already prohibits specified alien voting in federal-office elections, with the separately conducted authorized nonfederal-vote and parent/residence/reasonable-belief exceptions. H.R.884 extends a citizenship-based prohibition to the stated D.C. election/ballot scope and removes the local-law exception; it is not the first federal restriction on alien voting. It does not itself create naturalization, admission, removal or immigration-detention authority, prescribe a documentary-proof process, add a criminal penalty, or adjudicate the constitutional/enforcement consequences for an individual. H.Res.489 deems a pending committee substitute and provides a separate final-passage/recommit stage; this exact EH whole-bill passage has its own episode. Actual registration cancellation, ballot exclusion, crime, removal, loss of status, election effect or enactment is not inferred.

The exact June12,2025 House passage question concerns the complete S.331 ES. H.Res.489 section4 provides consideration of that bill as read, without deeming a substitute for S.331. Section2 proposes statutory Schedule I class coverage under its own definition,forms,exceptions and listing authority; the whole proposal also contains the remaining research,technical-reference,rulemaking,penalty and applicability provisions. House passage is distinct from Senate passage on March14 and later July enactment; no later public-law text is used as the June vote-time baseline.
The Immigration relationship is confined to the controlled-substance classification expressly incorporated by the identified grounds, rather than every criminal-law consequence. Under existing 8 U.S.C. 1182(a), subject to the chapter's exceptions, aliens inadmissible under the listed paragraphs are ineligible for visas and admission. Section 1182(a)(2)(A)(i)(II) retains conviction, admission of committing the offense, or admission of acts constituting its essential elements; a violation, conspiracy or attempt to violate a State, United States or foreign law or regulation relating to a controlled substance defined in 21 U.S.C. 802 is still required. The youth and petty-crime exceptions printed in clause (ii) apply to the moral-turpitude branch in clause (i)(I), not automatically to this controlled-substance branch. Section 1182(a)(2)(C)(i) separately requires the consular officer or Attorney General to know or have reason to believe the alien is or has been an illicit trafficker, knowing aider, abettor, assister, conspirator or colluder, or has endeavored to engage in the specified trafficking; it includes the separately printed listed-chemical alternative and does not substitute a conviction requirement for these tests. Clause (C)(ii) is governed by the SAME common governmental threshold: the consular officer or Attorney General must know or have reason to believe that the applicant is the spouse, son or daughter of an alien inadmissible under (C)(i), has obtained within the previous five years a financial or other benefit from that alien's illicit activity, and knew or reasonably should have known that the benefit came from that illicit activity. The governmental threshold and the recipient's own knowledge conditions are distinct and both remain; relationship alone does not suffice.
Under 8 U.S.C. 1227(a), an alien, including an alien crewman, IN AND ADMITTED TO THE UNITED STATES is subject to removal UPON THE ORDER OF THE ATTORNEY GENERAL if within a listed deportable class. Its controlled-substance conviction ground in 1227(a)(2)(B)(i) separately requires conviction at any time after admission for a violation, conspiracy or attempt to violate the identified State, United States or foreign law or regulation relating to a substance defined by 21 U.S.C. 802, except a single offense involving possession for one's own use of 30 grams or less of marijuana. Neither classification alone nor this House choice establishes an individual's deportability or produces an automatic removal order. The separate drug-abuser/addict ground in (B)(ii) is not given an express section 802 incorporation that it does not print. Existing 1182(h) allows only its separately qualified discretionary waiver, with the controlled-substance part confined to a single simple-possession offense involving 30 grams or less of marijuana and its other eligibility, exclusions and discretion preserved. Section 1182(d)(3)(A) separately permits qualified temporary nonimmigrant admission in the Attorney General's discretion, with recommendation/approval or documentation requirements and its printed exclusions and conditions; this is not an all-drug immigrant waiver or an entitlement. These grounds and waivers are not newly enacted or repealed by this proposal.
Section 802(6) defines a controlled substance through inclusion in Schedules I-V. The June 12, 2025 baseline already included temporary Schedule I class control under 21 C.F.R. 1308.11(h)(30). The original order ran February 6, 2018-February 6, 2020; Public Law 116-114 kept it in effect notwithstanding other law, and the April 2020 correction expressly preserved uninterrupted control despite the electronic-CFR omission, distinguishing effectiveness from applicability. The December2024 extension in Public Law118-158 section5105 ran through March31,2025. The later PRE-JUNE-VOTE Public Law119-4, enacted March15,2025, section3105 changed that endpoint to September30,2025, effective as if included in Public Law116-114. Thus the June choice is compared against existing temporary class control through September30,2025, not an expired March31order or first-ever class control. S.331 would ADD statutory Schedule I coverage without that temporary September 30 expiry, under its own definition and exceptions. It does not say it repeals or replaces temporary paragraph (h)(30), establish first-ever class control, or make every listed substance's status irrevocable. The source-supported proposed continuation of an expressly incorporated classification is the bounded domain mechanism; no universal criminal-law or collateral-consequence domain rule is accepted.
The temporary order prints isomers, esters, ethers, salts and salts of those forms, excluding substances under another DEA Controlled Substance Code Number and those with an FDA section 505 exemption or approval. S.331's proposed Schedule I(e)(1) instead prints its own material/compound/mixture/preparation and salts/isomers/salts-of-isomers language, unless specifically exempted or in another schedule. Its definition uses one or more of five specified structural modifications: phenyl-portion replacement in the phenethyl group, listed substitution in/on that group, listed substitution in/on the piperidine ring, replacement of the aniline ring with an aromatic monocycle, or replacement of the N-propionyl group by another acyl group. Paragraph (e)(3) excludes substances controlled by Attorney General action under section 201 or expressly listed in another schedule; the temporary FDA phrase is not repeated verbatim. The proposed class and temporary class are not declared identical chemical sets, and no particular medicine or substance is classified here. Medical fentanyl's existing Schedule II listing remains distinct; this is not moving all fentanyl into Schedule I. Existing scheduling/removal authority and the proposal's exemptions remain. An optional Attorney General list does not determine the status of every qualifying substance; absence from that list does not negate statutory control under the proposed definition.
The complete passage proposal also changes qualified research-registration procedures: an expedited route for investigational-exemption or specified HHS/Defense/VA-conducted/funded research, distinct notice/application timelines for already-registered and unregistered researchers, stated quantities and supplemental notices, and the preserved controlled-substance import/export requirements. The added303(n)(7)also requires a DOJ Inspector General study and report to Congress within one year of enactment about the paragraph2research with fentanyl; this is a reporting requirement, not an observed research result. It provides conditional shared institutional registration, qualified same-city/county sites under one institutional control with notices, inspection changes while retaining necessary anti-diversion inspections, conditional continuation after new Schedule I placement and specified hearing/application steps, small-quantity manufacturing incident to research with a marijuana-growing exclusion, and transparency for special research procedures. Those are not all researchers exempted from registration, unrestricted manufacturing or a new immigration admission rule. Technical dispensing-reference corrections, Attorney General rulemaking within six months with interim-final-rule/comment/hearing provisions, specified insertions of fentanyl-related substances into 21 U.S.C.841(b)(1) and 960(b) penalty provisions, and the section 802(60) class-definition cross-reference remain parts of the whole choice. Section 7(b) is a rule of construction concerning analogue treatment for those penalty provisions and pre-enactment conduct, not an automatic retroactive INA finding. The McCray reference is a sense-of-Congress statement, not proof of an actual case outcome. Yea or Nay concerns the WHOLE proposal, without identifying a separate component preference, motive or preferred alternative; the House result does not establish enactment, certification, a particular substance's classification, inadmissibility, deportability, removal or a realized health/enforcement effect.
