The exact H.R.2056 EH proposal prohibits the District of Columbia from having a statute, ordinance, policy or practice that prohibits or restricts a District government entity or official from sending, receiving, maintaining or exchanging information about any individual's citizenship or immigration status, lawful or unlawful, with any Federal, State or local government entity. It separately prohibits such District restrictions on compliance with a lawfully made DHS request under INA 236 or 287 to comply with a detainer for, or notify about release of, an individual. This is an express D.C.-specific restriction on governmental policies/practices. Existing 8 USC 1373 and 1644 already contain statutory restrictions on limiting certain status-information exchanges with the immigration service; the bill is not the first general permission to communicate immigration status. The bill's printed information clause includes citizenship as well as status and communication with any listed governmental entity, while its separate lawful-request clause specifically addresses detainers/release notices. INA 236 and 287 already govern qualified immigration custody and officer powers, including specified custody/release conditions, arrest limits and cooperation provisions. H.R.2056 does not itself rewrite those authorities, deem every DHS request lawful, or establish that every individual detainer must be obeyed. It bars District policies restricting the specified lawful-request compliance; individual custody legality, actual information disclosure/detention/removal, implementation and enactment are not inferred.

The complete H.R.1998 EH creates a conditional sanctions scheme separate from its findings and nonbinding global anti-piracy statements. The President must impose the described sanctions for a foreign person determined knowingly to engage in piracy. Foreign person excludes the printed U.S.-person categories: U.S. citizens, permanent resident aliens and U.S.-organized entities including foreign branches; unlike H.R.36 this definition does not exclude every person merely located in the United States. Section4(b)(1) property blocking is MAY despite the general SHALL in4(a), and dispenses with1701 emergency prerequisites. The immigration route applies to an INA alien whom State or DHS, or either designee, knows or has reason to believe is described in4(a): inadmissibility, no visa/entry documentation, no admission/parole or any other INA benefit. The issuing consular officer, State, DHS or a designee SHALL revoke the qualifying alien visa/entry documentation in accordance with existing INA221(i), regardless of issuance date, with immediate effect cancelling other valid entry documents. Existing221(i) already gives consular officers/State discretionary anytime revocation, notice to the Attorney General, invalidation from issuance, protected carrier reliance absent due notice, and the qualified judicial-review limitation/sole-ground removal-proceeding exception. The new targeted mandatory rule and listed DHS actor are not the first visa-revocation authority; the candidate does not infer repeal of the incorporated safeguards. Piracy expressly means ANY act violating ANY provision of18 USCchapter81, not only a violent seizure at sea. The chapter includes law-of-nations/high-seas piracy, citizenship/treaty-qualified foreign commissions or war, privateer arming/service, violent obstruction of a commander, vessel/property conversion or surrender, corrupt assistance/trading/confederacy, distress-vessel plunder, escape obstruction/false lights, malicious vessel attack, knowing receipt of pirate property and robbery ashore from a piratical cruise, each with its own elements/jurisdiction. These are existing predicates, not new criminal offenses or a claim that every offense can apply to every foreign person; the bill determination/knowledge test does not expressly require conviction. Necessary admission OR parole for UN-headquarters/other international obligations is excepted, with the printed reference to sanctions with respect to admission retained. Qualified agricultural/food/medicine/device, humanitarian, finance and necessary transport transactions are excepted, as are authorized U.S. intelligence, law-enforcement and national-security activities. No importation-of-goods sanctions authority is added and no family extension is stated. The President may waive sanctions after certifying to House Foreign Affairs and Senate Foreign Relations at least 15 days before effectiveness that the waiver is CRUCIAL to U.S. national-security interests; this bill states no 180-day maximum. Existing IEEPA implementation and penalties apply to specified regulatory violations, preserving criminal willfulness/conviction rather than equating sanctions designation with a criminal judgment. Classified evidence may be submitted ex parte/in camera in an existing judicial review, without creating a review right. The recorded suspension-and-passage as amended concerns the entire EH, a separate bill episode; no actual piracy, designation, visa cancellation, removal, enforcement outcome or enactment is inferred.

The exact H.R.875 EH proposal adds INA 212(a)(2)(J) inadmissibility for any alien convicted of, admitting commission of, or admitting acts constituting the essential elements of an intoxicated/impaired-driving offense. The terms take their meaning under the law of the jurisdiction where the conviction, offense or essential acts occurred, expressly including alcohol/drug influence or impairment, without regard to misdemeanor/felony classification under Federal, State, tribal or local law. Existing INA 212(a) makes inadmissibility relevant to visas and admission. It separately adds INA 237(a)(2)(G) deportability for conviction of a jurisdiction-defined intoxicated/impaired-driving offense, including alcohol/drug influence or impairment, regardless of the listed misdemeanor/felony classification. That clause uses the law where conviction occurred and does not make admission of conduct alone its predicate. Neither clause requires an injury/death or multiple offenses. The existing INA 101(a)(48) conviction framework remains, including specified withheld-adjudication situations with guilt/plea/facts and court-ordered punishment/penalty/restraint. These are additional categorical statutory grounds, rather than a claim that covered conduct previously could never trigger other criminal inadmissibility or deportability. Existing criminal INA grounds retain their own elements and exceptions. The single-offense minor/petty-offense exception in 212(a)(2)(A), the enumerated 212(h) waiver, and the 237(a)(2)(A)(vi) pardon exception are not printed exceptions to new J/G. Existing discretionary temporary-nonimmigrant/T/U inadmissibility waiver routes are retained within their own conditions; no categorical relief, guilt or automatic deportation is inferred. The bill concerns any alien meeting the grounds, not only a person unlawfully present. The new 237(a)(2) deportability ground sits within the existing 237(a) framework for an alien (including a crewman) in and admitted to the United States, with removal upon the specified government order. It is not a universal new deportability ground for every unadmitted alien. INA 101 distinguishes immigration admission (lawful entry after inspection/authorization) from admitting criminal conduct; parole alone is not admission. This governing status scope is separate from any offense's after-admission timing element. No individual admission status or actual removal order is inferred.

The exact H.R.275 EH proposal requires the DHS Secretary, by the seventh day of each month starting with the first full month after enactment, to publish a DHS webpage report and submit it to the House Homeland Security and Senate Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Committees. Each report must give the preceding month's total encounters of “special interest aliens”, their nationalities or countries of last habitual residence, geographic disaggregation, whether encounters occurred at land/air/sea ports of entry, between ports or in the U.S. interior, and identification of covered-nation nationalities/residences. The first report also covers January 20, 2021 through January 19, 2025. The operative definition is an INA-defined alien who, based on analysis of travel patterns, potentially poses a national-security risk to the United States or its interests. It does not establish an actual threat, criminal guilt, inadmissibility or removal for an individual. The incorporated covered nations are North Korea, China, Russia and Iran under 10 USC 4872(f)(2); only that definition is imported, not the unrelated procurement powers. The operative report covers DHS encounters, including the interior. The title's reference to attempts at unlawful entry does not create an unstated unlawful-entry-only reporting limit. This bill adds this specific recurring and retrospective reporting duty; it neither changes admission/removal eligibility nor authorizes new detention or spending. No actual report, encounter totals, threat finding or enactment is inferred.

This July3 House concurrence concerns the Senate's July1 EAS, which strikes all after the first word and replaces the earlier H.R.1 text. It is the complete multi-domain reconciliation replacement, not a second passage of the unchanged House bill or a separate vote on its Immigration components. Selected Immigration highlights here concern border infrastructure, detention and asylum fees; other immigration-related benefits, taxes, employment authorization, child-sponsor, reimbursement and enforcement provisions are not exhaustively described. Section90001 would appropriate an additional $46.55billion for fiscal2025 to CBP, available until September30,2029, for new/replacement primary, waterborne and secondary barriers, access roads, detection attributes and ground preparation for CBP operations and barrier construction/maintenance. The different House60001 accounts are not silently used to define this replacement amount or its purposes. Section90003 would appropriate an additional $45billion for fiscal2025 to ICE, available until September30,2029, for single-adult alien detention and family residential-center capacity. Aliens MAY be detained at family centers pending an INA removal decision and, if ordered removed, until removal. Single-adult detention standards are set in the Secretary's discretion CONSISTENT WITH APPLICABLE LAW. The family-center definition covers apprehended/encountered family units, including children who are not statutorily defined unaccompanied alien children, and does not reproduce the House's express regardless-of-State-licensing clause.6USC279(g)(2) requires no lawful immigration status, under18 age, and no US parent/legal guardian or none available for care/physical custody. Neither the capacity funding nor permission establishes automatic detention/removal of every alien, elimination of all legal constraints or actual operations. Section100002 requires an additional fee upon filing an asylum application. The fiscal2025 amount is the greater of $100 or the amount set by DHS/the Attorney General, as applicable, by rule; it cannot be waived/reduced. From fiscal2026 the prior fiscal-year fee is increased by the printed July-to-July CPI-U increment rounded down to a multiple of $10. Half of Attorney-General-filed receipts go to EOIR; half of DHS-filed receipts go to USCIS's existing Immigration Examinations Fee Account, retained/expended without further appropriation; uncredited receipts go to Treasury. This $100 filing floor differs from the House's $1,000 floor. Section100009 separately requires an additional fee for EACH CALENDAR YEAR an asylum application remains pending. Its fiscal2025 amount is the greater of $100 or a DHS rule amount, followed by the printed CPI-U annual adjustment with the increment rounded DOWN TO THE NEAREST DOLLAR; receipts go to Treasury and the fee cannot be waived/reduced. Do not transfer that rounding to the initial-filing fee or back to the House's differently printed yearly formula. Section100018 changes pre-vote INA208(d)(3)/8USC1158(d)(3) from MAY impose fees to SHALL and replaces the following cost-cap/installment/nonmandatory-fee language with preserved additional adjudication/naturalization-fee authority under286(m). The baseline already authorized asylum-consideration, employment-authorization and asylum-based adjustment fees;1356(m)/(n) govern existing account/cost-recovery context. No first-ever fee authority, new asylum eligibility test from that edit, specific implemented collection rule or actual payment is inferred. Employment-authorization fees are separate from asylum filing and annual pending-application fees. Senate100003 requires additional initial application fees for asylum applicants under1158(d)(2), paroled aliens andTPS employment-authorization applicants under1254a(a)(1)(B). Each fiscal2025 floor is$550 or a higher DHS rule amount, with no waiver/reduction and fiscal2026-onward July-to-July CPI-U increments rounded down to$10. The asylum-initial subsection contains no House-style six-month duration sentence; it credits25percent of fees collected PURSUANT TO THIS SUBSECTION to USCIS's existing fee account, retained/expended without further appropriation with NOT LESS THAN50percent of the credited share for benefit-fraud detection/prevention, and sends the rest to Treasury. Parole/TPS initial fees go to Treasury; their initial authorizations last one year or the duration of parole/TPS respectively, whichever is shorter. Senate100010 and100012 set separate parole/TPS employment-authorization renewal/extension fiscal2025 fee floors of$275, possible higher DHS rule amounts and later CPI increments rounded down to$10. Each sends25percent to USCIS's existing fee account to retain/spend without further appropriation and the rest to Treasury; no waiver/reduction.100012 states one year or the duration of the designation ofTPS, whichever is shorter.100010 literally says employment authorization for each paroled alien, OR ANY RENEWAL OR EXTENSION OF SUCH PAROLE, shall be valid for one year or parole duration, whichever is shorter. Preserve this printed antecedent and leave its application unresolved; do not rewrite it into a new parole-eligibility rule or import House six-month text. Senate100011 imposes at least$275 for each asylum-based employment-authorization renewal/extension, with25percent credited to USCIS's existing fee account without further appropriation, the rest to Treasury and no waiver/reduction. It prints no annual CPI formula or House-style six-month limit. It retains the three termination points: immediately after asylum-officer denial unless referred to an immigration judge;30days after immigration-judge denial unless timely appealed to BIA; immediately after BIA denies an appeal of asylum denial. It does not reproduce the separate House70013(d) prohibition on later grants/renewals/extensions absent a FederalCourtOfAppeals remand. Absence of that House sentence does not establish unlimited permission or erase other law. The complete pre-vote1158(d)(2) already permits regulated asylum-based work authorization while denying entitlement and preserving a180day wait for applicants not otherwise eligible. Existing1254a(a)(1)(B)/(a)(2) authorizes employment throughout TPS. Document-validity clauses do not themselves terminate TPS, create first employment authority or establish individual eligibility. Existing1182(d)(5)(A)/(B) preserves case-by-case temporary humanitarian/significant-public-benefit parole subject to the printed statutory exceptions, including its refugee qualification and the distinction from admission; paying a fee does not supply parole or work permission. Senate100016 requires a fiscal2025 fee of at least$5,000, or a higher DHS rule amount, on an alien BOTH ordered removed in absentia under1229a(b)(5) AND subsequently arrested by ICE, with fiscal2026-onward CPI-U increments rounded down to$10. It does not apply if the order was rescinded under1229a(b)(5)(C).50percent goes to ICE's Detention and Removal Office Fee Account, retained/expended without further appropriation; the rest goes to Treasury. It expressly bars waiver/reduction. These fee conditions preserve the underlying notice/address/removability proof, rescission, exceptional-circumstances definition and motion-to-reopen stay in complete pre-vote1229a(b)(5)/(e) and1229(a); an actual order/arrest, new removal ground or denied legal review is not inferred. Senate100017 separately requires an additional fee from any INADMISSIBLE alien at the time the person is apprehended BETWEEN PORTS OF ENTRY. Its fiscal2025 floor is$5,000 or a higher DHS rule amount, with later CPI-U increments rounded down to$10. Unlike House70022, this operative sentence does not name CBP as the apprehending actor. It prints TWO proceeds clauses: subsection(c) sends50percent to ICE's Detention and Removal Office Fee Account for retention/spending without further appropriation and the remainder to Treasury; subsection(d) says ALL fees under the section go to Treasury. The exact EAS HTML and officialPDF pages827-828 both print these clauses. The candidate preserves the apparent allocation conflict and does not choose an operative distribution. No express no-waiver clause is printed in100017; do not import100016(e) or House70022(d), or infer that a waiver is available. These are exact between-port/inadmissibility and in-absentia-plus-ICE-arrest fee predicates, not all enforcement encounters or a fee-imposed finding that an alien actually met any predicate. Senate100004 adds a parole-entry fee with fiscal2025floor$1,000 or higher DHS rule amount, subsequent CPI-U increments rounded down to$10 and Treasury disposition. Its exceptions require the alien to establish the parole reason to DHS's satisfaction on an INDIVIDUAL,CASE-BY-CASE basis; its no-waiver clause expressly preserves those exceptions. Senate own new 25F clause a: (a) Allowance of Credit.--In the case of an individual who is a citizen or resident of the United States (within the meaning of section 7701(a)(9)), there shall be allowed as a credit against the tax imposed by this chapter for the taxable year an amount equal to the aggregate amount of qualified contributions made by the taxpayer during the taxable year. Senate own new 25F clause b: (b) Limitations.-- (1) In general.--The credit allowed under subsection (a) to any taxpayer for any taxable year shall not exceed $1,700. (2) Reduction based on state credit.--The amount allowed as a credit under subsection (a) for a taxable year shall be reduced by the amount allowed as a credit on any State tax return of the taxpayer for qualified contributions made by the taxpayer during the taxable year. Senate own new 25F clause c: (c) Definitions.--For purposes of this section-- (1) Covered state.--The term `covered State' means one of the States, or the District of Columbia, that, for a calendar year, voluntarily elects to participate under this section and to identify scholarship granting organizations in the State, in accordance with subsection (g). (2) Eligible student.--The term `eligible student' means an individual who-- (A) is a member of a household with an income which, for the calendar year prior to the date of the application for a scholarship, is not greater than 300 percent of the area median gross income (as such term is used in section 42), and (B) is eligible to enroll in a public elementary or secondary school. (3) Qualified contribution.--The term `qualified contribution' means a charitable contribution of cash to a scholarship granting organization that uses the contribution to fund scholarships for eligible students solely within the State in which the organization is listed pursuant to subsection (g). (4) Qualified elementary or secondary education expense.--The term `qualified elementary or secondary education expense' means any expense of an eligible student which is described in section 530(b)(3)(A). (5) Scholarship granting organization.--The term `scholarship granting organization' means any organization-- (A) which-- (i) is described in section 501(c)(3) and exempt from tax under section 501(a), and (ii) is not a private foundation, (B) which prevents the co-mingling of qualified contributions with other amounts by maintaining one or more separate accounts exclusively for qualified contributions, (C) which satisfies the requirements of subsection (d), and (D) which is included on the list submitted for the applicable covered State under subsection (g) for the applicable year. Senate own new 25F clause d: (d) Requirements for Scholarship Granting Organizations.-- (1) In general.--An organization meets the requirements of this subsection if-- (A) such organization provides scholarships to 10 or more students who do not all attend the same school, (B) such organization spends not less than 90 percent of the income of the organization on scholarships for eligible students, (C) such organization does not provide scholarships for any expenses other than qualified elementary or secondary education expenses, (D) such organization provides a scholarship to eligible students with a priority for-- (i) students awarded a scholarship the previous school year, and (ii) after application of clause (i), any eligible students who have a sibling who was awarded a scholarship from such organization, (E) such organization does not earmark or set aside contributions for scholarships on behalf of any particular student, and (F) such organization-- (i) verifies the annual household income and family size of eligible students who apply for scholarships to ensure such students meet the requirement of subsection (c)(2)(A), and (ii) limits the awarding of scholarships to eligible students who are a member of a household for which the income does not exceed the amount established under subsection (c)(2)(A). (2) Prohibition on self-dealing.-- (A) In general.--A scholarship granting organization may not award a scholarship to any disqualified person. (B) Disqualified person.--For purposes of this paragraph, a disqualified person shall be determined pursuant to rules similar to the rules of section 4946. Senate own new 25F clause e: (e) Denial of Double Benefit.--Any qualified contribution for which a credit is allowed under this section shall not be taken into account as a charitable contribution for purposes of section 170. Senate own new 25F clause f: (f) Carryforward of Unused Credit.-- (1) In general.--If the credit allowable under subsection (a) for any taxable year exceeds the limitation imposed by section 26(a) for such taxable year reduced by the sum of the credits allowable under this subpart (other than this section, section 23, and section 25D), such excess shall be carried to the succeeding taxable year and added to the credit allowable under subsection (a) for such taxable year. (2) Limitation.--No credit may be carried forward under this subsection to any taxable year following the fifth taxable year after the taxable year in which the credit arose. For purposes of the preceding sentence, credits shall be treated as used on a first-in first-out basis. Senate own new 25F clause g: (g) State List of Scholarship Granting Organizations.-- (1) List.-- (A) In general.--Not later than January 1 of each calendar year (or, with respect to the first calendar year for which this section applies, as early as practicable), a State that voluntarily elects to participate under this section shall provide to the Secretary a list of the scholarship granting organizations that meet the requirements described in subsection (c)(5) and are located in the State. Senate own new 25F clause h: (h) Regulations and Guidance.--The Secretary shall issue such regulations or other guidance as the Secretary determines necessary to carry out the purposes of this section, including regulations or other guidance-- (1) providing for enforcement of the requirements under subsections (d) and (g), and (2) with respect to recordkeeping or information reporting for purposes of administering the requirements of this section.. Senate separate scholarship income exclusion: (b) Exclusion From Gross Income for Scholarships for Qualified Elementary or Secondary Education Expenses of Eligible Students.-- (1) In general.--Part III of subchapter B of chapter 1 is amended by inserting before section 140 the following new section: SEC. 139K. The complete January 12 H.R. 2683 EH suspension-and-passage proposal adds remote access to the Export Control Reform Act framework. New section 1742(15) defines remote access as access on a purposeful, knowing, reckless OR negligent basis to an item subject to U.S. jurisdiction under the Act BY A FOREIGN PERSON through a network connection, including internet/cloud services, FROM A LOCATION OTHER THAN THE ITEM'S PHYSICAL LOCATION, IF Commerce determines that use of the item could pose a SERIOUS national-security or foreign-policy risk. Neither overseas location, China connection nor a particular AI model is printed as a universal trigger. Items include commodities, software and technology; the item/risk/jurisdiction/network/different-location/foreign-person conditions matter. Ordinary internet use or every cloud service is not automatically prohibited, and the bill does not supply a specific new list of controlled models, devices, countries or individual licenses.
The material Immigration boundary is the direct natural-person eligibility predicate, not national-security rhetoric or predicted immigration consequences. Existing 4801(5)(A) expressly excludes from foreign person a U.S. citizen, a LAWFUL PERMANENT RESIDENT, or another protected individual under8 U.S.C. 1324b(a)(3). The imported definition covers citizens OR nationals and specified LPR, lawful temporary residence under 1160(a)/1255a(a)(1), refugee and asylum statuses, with its naturalization application/pursuit/time qualifications. LPR exclusion is also an INDEPENDENT explicit route in4801(5)(A); a qualification on the imported protected-individual route does not erase that separate LPR exclusion. Not all foreign-born people, noncitizens, visa holders or persons physically in the United States have the same covered status. Immigration/nationality status directly affects whether a natural person is the foreign recipient of the newly regulated access; it does not grant or alter that immigration status, naturalization, visas, work authorization or INA admission/removal. Importing the definition does not import all employment-discrimination remedies, exemptions or a right to employment. The entity branch separately includes defined non-U.S.-incorporated/organized businesses and other entities, international organizations, foreign governments/agencies; that branch is not an immigration-status determination about every employee, owner or national. Existing 4801(13)U.S. person includes, for subchapterI, qualified nationals/protected individuals, organized legal entities AND any person IN THE UNITED STATES; U.S. person and foreign person are not simple complements. Providers and other U.S. persons can have duties even when they are not foreign-person recipients. No unrestricted-access entitlement for every citizen/LPR or blanket criminal exemption is established.
The proposal adds risk-qualified foreign-person remote access to the President's SHALL-control authority and the corresponding SHALL-regulate duty in4812, carried out through established policy objectives and the framework for regulations, controlled-item/person/end-use lists and guidance. It extends Commerce's existing 4813 prohibitions on UNAUTHORIZED transfers, restrictions for listed foreign persons/end uses, licensing/conditions/suspension/revocation, foreign-availability assessment, compliance/information, inspection/seizure/temporary denial, monitoring, license-required notice and enhanced controls to the specified remote-access settings. This is regulatory authority and specified duties, not an immediate statutory ban on every covered access, mandatory denial of every foreign person's application or a free license for excluded natural persons. Separate extended enhanced controls apply to U.S. persons and the named weapons/nuclear-project activities, with retained material-contribution denial standard and other-agency authorization exception. Existing 4813(b) retains the IEEPA 1702(b)limits on items that cannot be regulated, including qualified personal communications, humanitarian articles, information/materials and travel transactions, with the printed donation determinations/information-control exceptions. No universal exemption for every data/model/software transaction or repeal of other sanctions/export authorities is inferred. Existing terrorism-country licensing has its country/item/State determinations and30-day congressional notice; it is not a new immigration visa ground or a citizenship-wide country ban.
H.R. 2683 extends the existing interagency person-list/end-use monitoring criteria, Commerce licensing/authorization procedure, prospective compliance assistance, penalties, enforcement/confidentiality and interagency control-coordination clauses. Retained expeditious/transparent licensing and no-application-fee framework matters; the thirty-day processing wording is a SENSE OF CONGRESS best-efforts standard, not automatic approval or a newly imposed hard thirty-day deadline. Existing compliance assistance/security-clearance provisions are not new immigration-clearance or visa powers. The new congressional-consultation section requires Commerce to keep House Foreign Affairs and Senate Banking committees fully/currently informed of anticipated remote-access regulations, including risk, method and economic effect, in classified settings as necessary. It expressly does NOT require their approval as a condition of exercising ECRA authority. No public disclosure of classified information or committee veto is created.
The definition's purposeful/knowing/reckless/negligent range expressly does NOT lower criminal mens rea under section 1760. Existing 4819(b) WILLFUL criminal violation/attempt/conspiracy or aiding/abetting framework, statutory maximum fine of $1 million and individual imprisonment up to 20 years, including the printed AND and OR BOTH clause, is retained rather than new strict-liability imprisonment for negligent access. Those are statutory maxima, not a current inflation-adjusted civil-dollar quote or an individual sentence. Civil authority can include fine, license revocation and extended ability-to-access/provide-access prohibition, with notice/opportunity for agency hearing. The specified false-document/report and remote-access provisions are within the retained unlawful-act framework. Existing prior-CONVICTION authority is DISCRETIONARY: it may deny remote-access/provision eligibility for ANY item, WHETHER OR NOT controlled, for up to 10 years or revoke interested licenses for the listed offenses; related-party extension requires a shown affiliation/ownership/control/responsibility/trade connection and retained hearing procedures. It is not automatic guilt or immigration removal of family members. Existing criminal/civil forfeiture and other administrative/judicial/settlement powers remain context, not a new INA consequence. Enforcement search/detain/seize/temporary-denial authorities concern covered items/conveyances and suspected control violations; they do not create new immigration detention/removal authority because DHS can participate. Confidential licensing/reporting/enforcement information retains specified withholding/national-interest, Congress/GAO and qualified interagency sharing rules.
Complete affected ECRA sections4801/4811-16/4819-20/4825, the material IEEPA limits and protected-status definition were independently read from official primary baselines. Their 2024 Code/as of January 6, 2025 capture labels are preserved; no universal subsequent-law currency, current regulation, actual license determination or administrative outcome is claimed. This is one whole H.R. 2683 suspension-and-passage choice and bill episode. The status-predicate cross-domain boundary and actual regulatory application remain explicit independent-review questions; no ontology expansion, editorial acceptance or production eligibility is conferred. Yea supports the complete authority/oversight proposal; Nay opposes it without establishing a preferred alternative, motive, model restriction, employee's status or an actual border outcome.

The January 22 H.R. 7147 PASSAGE choice uses the complete IH body AS AMENDED by adopted H.Res. 1014 section 7, which adds the Senate-data 213 repeal before passage. The rule permits explanatory material by January 23 and directs later incorporation into H.R. 7148; the annual appropriation clauses themselves name the Final Bill table. The LATER H.Res. 1016 engrossment correction must not be back-projected: as voted,230(b) bars procurement/equipping of long-range kinetic-capable unmanned aircraft using THIS ACT OR ANY OTHER ACT funds; the later EH instead limits that phrase to DHS funds in this/prior Acts. The House passage record and correction sequence are separately bound. The standalone printed reference to consolidated-Act section 4 and subsequent packaging/report implementation are preserved for independent candidate legal review rather than treated as an unprinted stand-alone section. This action shares the H.R. 7147 episode with the later whole House CR replacement, each with its own meaning and actual choice. The annual DHS titles would fund existing border processing/security, immigration enforcement, custody and removal, citizenship-services processing and verification, and associated oversight for FY 2026 within a wider DHS package. CBP Operations and Support is $17.727974 billion, with $550 million available through September 30, 2027, mixed customs/trade/travel, UAC transport, air/marine and law-enforcement functions, Harbor Maintenance and user-fee components, and qualified informant, preclearance and Tribal-road uses. CBP procurement/construction is $222.886 million with distinct September 2028 asset and September 2030 construction availability. The final table allocates CBP Ops across Border Security $6.644912 billion, Trade/Travel $6.610801 billion, Integrated Operations $1.730551 billion and Mission Support $2.741710 billion; these are not four independently voted immigration policies or all-person-removal spending. The earlier $650 million CBP-to-FEMA shelter-transfer row has no new Final Bill amount. ICE Ops is $10.036362 billion, including $46.696 million through September 2027, no-year forced-labor funds, qualified HERO/IP-rights/informant/special-operations uses and up to $11.216 million for care, maintenance and repatriation of smuggled aliens UNLAWFULLY PRESENT. The final allocations are HSI $2.591251 billion, ERO $5.453706 billion, Mission Support $1.543711 billion and OPLA $447.694 million. USCIS Ops is $122.941 million: $112.566 million Employment Status Verification and $10.375 million Application Processing/backlog reduction in the Final Bill table, not exclusively E-Verify. OSEM Ops $316.295 million includes $10 million CRCL, $5 million Citizenship/Immigration Services Ombudsman, no new Immigration Detention Ombudsman allocation, and no new $15 million ATD Case Management Grant allocation; the last two do not abolish their statutory offices or all ATD. OBIM receives $271 million and IDENT/HART procurement $25 million. The wider TSA, Coast Guard, Secret Service, disaster, cyber, training, research, Supreme Court-security and air-traffic provisions remain whole-package context; membership in DHS does not make all their spending Immigration evidence.

The statutory restrictions preserve their exact funding and trigger scopes. Section 207 bars a NEW defined land-border crossing fee and a related study, beginning enactment, for pedestrians/cyclists/private-vehicle drivers/passengers at northern/southern LPOEs; it does not abolish all existing immigration or inspection fees.208 requires a 90 day CBP procurement plan before this Act's funds are obligated;209 permits altering National Targeting Center operations but protects planned vetting at existing locations across specified current/prior/fee funds unless later statute authorizes a reduction.210 bars funds for Border Security Assets/Infrastructure in this or prior Acts from procuring/deploying NONAUTONOMOUS surveillance SYSTEMS, using 119-21 section 90004(c)'s definition; the older 90004(b) restriction separately concerns tested/accepted autonomous TOWERS using that section's funds.211 requires the November 30, 2021 CBP pregnant/postpartum/nursing/infant custody policy OR substantively similar standards developed with maternal/pediatric experts to be in effect and fully implemented. The original covered populations include pregnancy with medical concerns OR third trimester/active labor, nursing individuals, postpartum within six months or recent pregnancy loss, and infants under one year. Health interviews/assessment/referral retain resource/operational and offered-assessment/acceptance qualifications; documented fifteen-minute welfare checks, nutrition/breastfeeding/infant supplies, facility/operational qualifications and incident records remain; it is not first-ever care, an automatic 72 hour release rule, or identical unqualified entitlements for every person.212 prohibits using ICE Ops to CONTINUE 287(g) delegations when the DHS IG determines a MATERIAL agreement violation.213 prohibits continuing a detention-services contract if its TWO most recent OVERALL performance evaluations are BELOW adequate/equivalent median, with ICE OPR conducting the evaluations. Neither trigger is every complaint or one failed component score.214 permits necessary ICE Ops reprogramming/transfers for detention of aliens prioritized for removal without 503(d)'s time/condition limit; it is not an unrestricted waiver of every appropriation or statutory restriction.

215 continues semimonthly 2021 detention-data reporting, including the original 2020 operational/ATD/facility/detention/release/removal data and 2021 additions such as solitary-confinement use/duration and length-of-stay bins.216 reapplies complete 2020 sections 216/217: no covered detention/removal/referral/initiation-of-proceeding of a UAC sponsor, potential sponsor or household member BASED ON HHS-shared information, EXCEPT the specified background-check findings of an aggravated-felony/child-abuse/sexual-violence/child-porn felony conviction OR pending related FELONY charge, business association involving unrelated minors below legal wage or denied school, or prostitution participation/implementation. It is neither an absolute sponsor exemption nor an exception for every conviction or illegal-entry suspicion. The retained 2020 section 217 report is submitted by the ICE Director, not the Inspector General. It requires participating jurisdictions' community outreach, counts of individuals placed in removal proceedings, state/local officers' performance data including nationality and criminality, and future agreement-expansion plans. The complete retained report's enumerated fields do not include training. This retained report is distinct from the current Act's section 217 budget plan.217 replaces the earlier 45 day current-Act plan with a 30 day Director briefing/written plan covering ALL available current/prior/carryover/fee funds, monthly PPA/pay/nonpay projections and unchanged initial comparison; monthly updates are due within 15 days after the following month begins. Conditional $100,000 Executive Leadership/Oversight amounts become available on the 16 th of each month, at most $700,000 for the fiscal year, subject to timely reporting beginning 30 days after enactment.218 requires a 90 day plan for 119-21 detention-facility funding, locations/beds/cost/transport/removal-flight/end-state capacity, with quarterly updates within 30 days; reporting projections are not observed immigration outcomes.219 protects ICE attaché/liaison presence at foreign embassies/consulates using this or other Act funds, except the joint DHS/State foreign-policy explanation or a host-country cessation request.238 reapplies the 2021 fencing restriction WITH RESPECT TO THIS ACT's funds in the same manner: Santa Ana, Bentsen-Rio Grande Valley State Park, La Lomita, National Butterfly Center, within OR EAST of Vista del Mar Ranch, and historic cemeteries. Do not infer an unrestricted prohibition on every separate reconciliation-fund use.

USCIS 401 permits only five replacement vehicles where GSA does not lease, with authorized home/work use;402 restricts A-76 competition for five named USCIS employee classes, including temporary/term staff;403 permits collection/use of biometrics at Application Support Centers overseen VIRTUALLY by USCIS personnel using appropriate technology. This repeats existing 2024 authority, rather than first authorizing biometrics, universal remote adjudication or unrestricted searches.512 continues the THIS ACT funding restriction on amending the INA 337 naturalization oath, preserving 1448's existing qualifying modified oaths and disability/qualifying-child waivers;517 uses 1324 a(h)(3)'s employment-at-the-particular-time definition, excluding LPRs and law-authorized workers from unauthorized alien, not all noncitizens.514 restricts this Act's funds for national-ID planning/testing/piloting/development, not every immigration identity document.527 continues the funding restriction on restraints for pregnant or post-delivery women in DHS custody/transport/outside treatment, with individualized unavoidable serious flight risk/immediate harm or therapeutic-medical exceptions for a pregnant woman, safest/least-restrictive provider-determined restraints, an ABSOLUTE active-labor/delivery ban, barred pregnant positions/belts and feasible left-side positioning.528 protects covered death/possible-sexual-assault/abuse records and allegations of abuse/crime/disruption BY detainees from destruction, with disclosure on an affected punished individual's request under applicable law/litigation rules. It is not unrestricted public access to all detainee or staff records.536 repeats a this/other-Act funding bar on transferring/releasing/assisting transfer to or within the United States/territories/possessions of the specified Guantanamo DOD-held-on-or-after-June 24, 2009 NONcitizen/NONmilitary detainees, not a general new INA inadmissibility ground for all people held elsewhere.547 bars THIS ACT DHS funds from blocking Members or designated House/Senate employees conducting oversight of DHS-operated/contracted ALIEN detention/housing facilities or restaging conditions: Members need no prior notice; staff may be required 24 hours. It is not an unrestricted public-visitor right or a blanket rule for all HHS facilities/funding sources.

General appropriation controls remain:501 current-fiscal-year obligation limit unless express longer/no-year availability;502 merges prior balances for the original purposes/availability;503 advance reprogramming notices and 5 percent transfers/no more than 10 percent augmentation, June 15 initial-notification limit with imminent-life/property exception, grant/new-unapproved-PPA restrictions and deobligated-balance procedures.503(f) permits UP TO $20 million transferred into the EXISTING Immigration Emergency Fund with five-day notice. The old 404 note separately authorizes a $35 million BALANCE and qualified immigration-emergency withdrawals needing Presidential determination/certification, plus capped State/local reimbursements under 404(b)(2) for which that emergency determination is not needed. S.-person interviews require factual reasonable belief in significant foreign intelligence; the definition includes known LPRs and qualified associations/corporations, with foreign-controlled-corporation exception. Legal/privacy/civic oversight and specified lawful information sharing are expressly preserved. It is not a general no-intelligence rule or new immigration status ground.

The January 22 explanatory narrative and visually checked FINAL BILL tables govern the named allocations; earlier House Report 119-173 PROPOSAL amounts and numbered proposed riders are not substituted for this actual text. The narrative says House report LANGUAGE has equal weight unless noted or addressed to the contrary, and repetition does not negate it unless expressly provided. Its operative directions include 287(g) cost-benefit/training/agreement evaluations and reports; border/credible-fear/parole/UAC/parent/veteran/tribal/arrest/removal/wrongful-return data; warrants/probable-cause/flight-risk reports; HART/IDENT oversight and qualified child-separation notifications; medical/water/food/shelter/TEDS and continued migrant-care requirements; free confidential ICE counsel communication/document/VAV access and legal-orientation continuation TO THE MAXIMUM EXTENT POSSIBLE; qualified family-unity/separation, pregnant-custody redeterminations and sensitive-location directions; facilities/segregation/inspections/PREA oversight; ATD metrics/consequence reporting, monitoring-feasibility and procurement directions; and USCIS processing dashboards/backlogs, fees/waivers, asylum/refugee/EAD/SIJ/H-2 A/H-2 B/R-1 processing/abuse and policy-change reporting. The separately incorporated 118-85,116-458 and 118-553 directions are source-bound, retaining their population/exception/scheduling/privacy/feasibility wording and distinguishing requested reports, encouraged actions, directives and statutory rights. For example, the port-of-entry counsel paragraph requests a 90 day briefing on requirements for a meaningful one-hour consultation for U. S. nationals, LPRs returning from a temporary foreign visit, valid unexpired immigrant/nonimmigrant visa holders, refugees, returning asylees or approved parole applicants, with greatest-practicable in-person advocacy, not an unconditional new lawyer entitlement for every border entrant. The related ICE counsel direction concerns free confidential unmonitored 60 minute calls/video with 24 hour scheduling, document exchange/delivery and facility access, not government-paid representation. Continued family reunification is qualified by best interests/possibility; the pregnancy-custody direction preserves required-law/exceptional-circumstance grounds and monthly review. The House TPS-Venezuela direction calls for reconsideration/analysis and a 30 day briefing, while the Ukraine program language urges continuation; neither itself grants a named person TPS/parole or first changes individual eligibility. The final fee-waiver language supersedes the House cost-recovery restriction while mandatory statutory fees and their own waiver limits are not silently repealed. The Housereport 50,000-bed proposal, earlier PPA figures and former numbered proposed sanctuary/rhetoric riders are not treated as actual present statutory conditions merely because the report is referenced. Conflicting or uncertain application of retained report language versus the final allocation/statutory scope remains a candidate-review question, not an accepted adjudication.

Baseline: 119-4 incorporated FY 2024 DHS 118-47 division C with specified exceptions/anomalies, including ICE's $9.986542 billion FY 2025 Ops level; at the January 22 vote, 119-37 division A carried relevant FY 2025 rates/conditions with its own exceptions and its printed January 30, 2026 outer date. Public Law 119-75 was enacted February 3, 2026, AFTER this exact House action; its February 13 continuing-resolution date is later chronology context only and must not govern the January choice. The annual proposal replaces the relevant continuation with full FY 2026 DHS appropriations; many sponsor/contract/287(g)/fencing/oath/employment/restraint/oversight/biometric controls already existed and are not first-ever rights or powers. The separate 119-21 reconciliation appropriations and fees are not all repealed/replaced by these annual totals. Whole passage includes enforcement funds, services, protective limits, oversight and other DHS/non-DHS provisions together. No component-only preference, motive, actual detention/deportation/care improvement, pay/spending, later enactment or individual legal outcome is inferred.

The exact H.J.Res.72 EH proposition terminates the national emergency identified by the President's February 1, 2025 finding in Executive Order 14193, using National Emergencies Act section 202. Under 50 USC 1622(a), powers or authorities exercised by reason of that identified emergency cease after termination, subject to savings for prior actions and unfinished proceedings, actions based on earlier acts, and matured rights/duties or incurred penalties. EO 14193 section 1 both expands the scope of the earlier southern-border emergency and declares/reiterates an NEA/IEEPA emergency concerning Canada. Its operative package imposes Canadian-product tariffs and related customs/foreign-trade-zone measures, assigns implementation/reporting duties, and in section 3(b) requires the DHS Secretary, coordinating with the specified officials, to recommend additional action if Canada fails to take adequate steps to alleviate illegal migration and illicit-drug crises through cooperative enforcement actions. That immigration-specific governmental recommendation duty is operative text, not merely a preamble prediction. Independent Immigration membership rests on terminating the identified emergency authority and its direct immigration-cooperation governance, without importing every mechanism from the earlier southern-border proclamation. The January 2026 continuation notice describes the emergencies as declared or expanded and continues the separately named instruments. This does not resolve every legal consequence of their overlapping emergency scopes. The candidate does not claim that the resolution independently repeals every January 20 military, detention, barrier or INA authority, orders Canada to cooperate, removes all tariffs under other authority, or changes an individual's immigration status. The underlying general NEA termination/savings framework and IEEPA authorities are retained; the proposed change is termination of this identified emergency rather than a new immigration power. The House choice concerns the complete emergency-termination proposition, including its trade and other purposes, rather than a separate vote on a particular tariff, recommendation or immigration program. Actual termination, executive action, tariff effects, cooperation, admission, detention, removal or enactment is not established by the House vote.

The February 11 House passage of S. 1383 adopts the complete SAVE America replacement in EAH, not the veterans-advisory body named in the retained Clerk title. The independently read RCP 119-19, Report 119-493 amendments and H.Res. 1057 section 6 correction establish the as-voted body: complete official voter-list comparison; absent-uniformed-services registration exception; broader final absent-uniformed-services absentee exception including qualified spouses/dependents and absence from residence rather than only overseas; removal of the extra State-selected government-ID category; immediate photo-rule effectiveness rather than original 2027 timing. Whole replacement passage is a separate S. 1383 bill episode; neither April 2025 H.R. 22 passage nor later post-passage NDAA packaging is a new component choice here.
Section 2 replaces NVRA section 4(b)'s existing continuously-qualified no-registration/same-day-registration State exemptions with documentary citizenship requirements for any registration method and adds a special confirmation system for a State/jurisdiction that does not require registration. NVRA State means the fifty States and DC; Federal-office scope is not every local election. Documentary proof has five alternative routes: citizenship-indicating REAL ID identification; valid U.S. passport; official military ID TOGETHER WITH military service record showing U.S. birth; valid Federal/State/Tribal photo ID showing U.S. birth; or other such photo ID TOGETHER WITH specified certified birth record, contemporaneous hospital extract, final adoption decree, Consular Report/certification of citizen birth abroad, naturalization/citizenship or other Federal INA proof, or DHS KIC card. The certified birth-record route has all listed issuer/file/name/date/place/parent/signature/seal requirements. Military ID alone is not the citizenship-proof route. REAL ID law permits many noncitizen statuses: the bill's first route additionally requires an indication of citizenship, not any compliant ID. Existing 22 U.S.C. 212 permits passports for noncitizen nationals; the literal valid-passport route is preserved alongside the citizenship requirement, without deciding individual eligibility or equating national with citizen. INA alien excludes both citizens and nationals; noncitizen and alien are not interchangeable.
The proposal requires acceptance/processing for a name discrepancy when otherwise qualifying proof is accompanied by required name-change documentation OR the State-process affidavit of prior name. Applicants without the listed documentary proof have a State process: sworn citizen/eligible attestation, OTHER EVIDENCE, official sufficiency determination and an official uniform EAC affidavit explaining the basis. Other discrepancies have an additional-documentation process. Attestation alone is not automatic registration. Motor-vehicle/agencies/mail forms and verification are amended; mail registration requires in-person proof at the election office by the State deadline or at a qualifying same-day polling place by election day, with notice/instructions and reasonable disability accommodations. New absent-uniformed-services applicants under 20310(1) are excepted from section 2 requirements; that defined category includes qualified service/merchant-marine members and their spouses/dependents absent from residence by reason of service, not every civilian overseas citizen. The State exemption savings concerns OTHER Federal laws, not retention of the replaced NVRA exemption. Registration amendments take effect at enactment for applications submitted on/after enactment.
Within 30 days States must establish ongoing citizenship-checking programs, submit their COMPLETE official Federal voter list to DHS for SAVE comparison and take removal steps after NOTICE and OPPORTUNITYto provide citizenship proof; a preexisting purpose-qualified DHSagreement may satisfy this duty. Other State data are optional, and Social Security-agreement information cannot be the SOLEground for removing a voter. Existing 405(r)(9) matches name/date/SSN/deceased records and has confidentiality/exception restrictions; no infallible citizenship database or individual noncitizenship is established. Federal departments possessing relevant eligibility information must provide necessary verification information, including requested batches, within 24 hours of a State request, share information and not charge the State a response fee. Printed SAVEresponse paragraph(1) reference and information-sharing paragraph(A) reference remain literal, not silently repaired. DHS SHALL investigate WHETHER to initiatesection 239 removal proceedings if an ALIEN is determined pursuant to the specified information provisions to be unlawfully registered for Federal elections. This is not automatic removal, conviction, investigation of every noncitizen list match or a new universal deportation ground. Existing section 239 notice/counsel/proceeding distinctions remain; existing 121(c)(1) noncriminal-enforcement-use bar creates an explicit review dependency, not an assumed repeal.
Section 2 adds noncitizen documentation/verified-information roll-removal grounds and at-any-time language, with the specified 90-day-systematic-removal exception amendment. List deletion is distinct from immigration removal. Mail form document-recording and qualified criminal/immigration evidentiary confidentiality exceptions are printed separately: motor-vehicle exception uses KNOWING attempts/false declarations, while mail exception omits those express words. Private civil enforcement adds missing-proof registration to covered violations but retains notice/cure and existing remedies. The amended 20511(2) criminal mechanism retains KNOWING AND WILLFUL fair-election deprivation/fraud/attempt elements; new executive-branch material assistance and missing-proof registration categories do not create strict-liability imprisonment for every mistaken official. Existing penalty is fine and/or up to five years. EAC registration guidance is due 10 days after enactment; voter-material development/modification is exempted from PRA; DHS must promptly notify the domicile State chief election official upon receiving naturalization information. Section 2 preserves provisional casting and counting if citizenship is verified under the new process, without waiving separate photo-ID ballot rules. Existing Federal alien-voting prohibition under section 611 and its mixed-election/qualified-belief exceptions are baseline, not newly created or repealed.
Section 3 adds HAVA section 303A photo-identification requirements for Federal ballots, not citizenship conferred by possessing photo ID. An in-person voter needs valid PHYSICAL photo ID; lacking it permits a provisional ballot but eligibility determination requires within THREE DAYS either the required ID or the State affidavit of religious objection to being photographed. Other reasons for provisional voting remain governed by their existing rules. A voter other than in person must submit an IDcopy OR last four SSN digits PLUS State affidavit of inability to obtain a copy after REASONABLE efforts. Exceptions are defined absent-uniformed-services voters and the specific 20102(b)(2)(B)(ii) alternative for an elderly/disabled voter assigned an inaccessible polling place after required findings/advance request; not every elderly/disabled or overseas voter. Final IDlist has ONLY five categories: valid State driver license with photo/expiration; State-motorvehicle-issued IDcard with photo/expiration; valid U.S. passport; valid military ID; valid Tribal photo ID with expiration. The deleted additional State-selected government-ID category is not restored; an ordinary student ID is not independently a listed route, without claiming students cannot vote. State/local officials must, TO THE EXTENT PRACTICABLE, provide no-cost copying-device access at government buildings; this does not require free IDissuance or universal device availability. Registration applicants, including online applicants before completion, receive photo-rule notices.
HAVA State has its own retained definition including DC, Puerto Rico, Guam, American Samoa and U.S. Virgin Islands; it is not silently replaced by the NVRA definition or made an exhaustive determination of every territorial election. The proposal extends AG civil enforcement to subtitle A of Title III. Complete Public Law 118-106 corroborates that existing HAVA section 304 is election-observer access, codified at 52 U.S.C. 21083a; Code numbering 21083a does NOT mean existing HAVA section 303A or a collision with the proposed photo-ID section. Section 3 and its nested photo-rule effective dates are enactment/elections on or after, not 2027. But the new EAC voluntary photo-guidance recommendation deadline is printed OCTOBER 1, 2025, before this February 2026 choice; no repaired prospective deadline or delayed effectiveness is inferred. Actual enactment, implementation, removals, eligibility, turnout, access outcomes, motives or preferred alternative are not established. Literal references, document/alternative-process/enforcement interactions, SAVE use and stale guidance timing remain candidate-review questions.

The complete H.R. 2189 EH adds a narrowly defined less-than-lethal projectile-device exception to the second sentence of 18 USC 921(a)(3), alongside its pre-existing antique-firearm exception, and adds paragraph (39). This is not solely a label for general criminal enforcement: existing INA 237(a)(2)(C) expressly incorporates FIREARM OR DESTRUCTIVE DEVICE as defined in 921(a), and existing 922(g)(5) regulates firearms/ammunition using illegal or unlawful presence or admission under a nonimmigrant visa. The candidate domain connection is those express definition/status links, not presumed immigration consequences from a crime. The firearm branch of the incorporated definition would acquire the new exception. The separate 921(a)(4) destructive-device definition is NOT amended by TitleI, and the INA ground separately includes destructive devices; a qualifying-device label therefore does not establish exemption from every branch or every other immigration ground. Existing 237(a)applies to an alien IN AND ADMITTED TO the United States, with removal upon the specified order, and 237(a)(2)(C)requires an after-admission CONVICTION under any law of the specified purchase/sale/exchange/use/ownership/possession/carrying or attempt/conspiracy conduct involving a qualifying weapon, part or accessory in violation of law. Arrest, allegation or a conduct admission alone is not this conviction predicate. No individual device classification, state-conviction comparison, adjudication, cancellation of an existing order or actual avoidance of removal is inferred. The new device must satisfy ALL printed criteria: not designed/intended to expel, nor readily convertible to accept/discharge, common handgun/rifle/shotgun ammunition or any other projectile above 500 feet/second; designed/intended use not likely to cause death or serious bodily injury; and unable to accept or be readily modified to accept a feeding device loaded through a pistol grip or commonly used in semiautomatic firearms. It is not every less-lethal weapon, every projectile device or a universal harmlessness finding. The AG must make a requested device determination within 90 days AFTER RECEIVING THE DEVICE; the deadline is not automatic approval or compulsory classification of every product. Existing 922(g)(5) and (y) status predicates, hunting/sport/license, foreign-official and friendly-government law-enforcement exceptions and qualified AG waiver remain baseline; not all noncitizens are prohibited. Existing ammunition is separately defined by 921(a)(17), so the proposal is not a blanket permission to possess otherwise regulated ammunition or ordinary firearms. It confers no nationality, visa, lawful presence, admission, work authorization or unrestricted weapons right. TitleII separately adds 4181 excise-tax exemptions for the defined devices, devices on the Secretary annual list meeting the criteria except the above 500 velocity criterion, and specified shells/cartridges with the printed design/use conditions; adds 90 day classification duties, annual lists/reports, and expands the distinct 5845(a)NFA definition exclusions to those device categories. The TAX listed-above 500 category is not inserted into TitleI 921(a)(39) and cannot be imported into the INA firearm-definition exception. Section 202 sales apply after enactment; qualifying requests in the first 180 days are treated as received at the close of that period for the 90 day rule. No special retroactive immigration/conviction rule is printed. Existing 4182 military, small-manufacturer and paid-NFA exemptions, existing 5845 antique/qualified collector-device exclusions, and enacted 119-21 section 70436 zero transfer/making-tax and 4182(a)conforming provisions are retained context, so this is not the first federal device exemption or tax relief and not a claim every affected product previously paid the same tax. These are distinct criminal, immigration-incorporation and tax objects. The exact whole-bill final-passage choice includes BOTH titles, not a separate vote on the removal ground, noncitizen possession or an individual device. One H.R. 2189 episode; the failed 1042 and adopted 1057 rules only established proposed/pending consideration and do not add independent policy findings. No actual sales, tax savings, public-safety effect or enactment is inferred.

The complete H.R. 6472 EH proposal adds HEA section 135A. A PUBLIC institution of higher education RECEIVING ASSISTANCE under the HEA must not charge a covered individual tuition OR fees above the rate charged for residents of the State WHERE THE INSTITUTION IS LOCATED. Covered individuals must satisfy BOTH residence in Guam, the Commonwealth of the Northern Mariana Islands, American Samoa or the U.S. Virgin Islands AND U.S. nationality as defined by INA 101(a)(22). That definition includes U.S. citizens and noncitizens owing permanent allegiance to the United States. Residence alone, lawful permanent residence alone or a visa alone does not establish the required nationality; this proposal does not confer nationality, citizenship, immigration status or naturalization. The four covered-residence jurisdictions are a specific list; Puerto Rico, the District of Columbia and the Freely Associated States are not added to that beneficiary-residence list. The HEA institution-location definition of State is broader: it includes the several States, Puerto Rico, DC, the four named territories and the Freely Associated States (Marshall Islands, Federated States of Micronesia and Palau). That institutional definition must not expand the covered-residence list or be collapsed to only the fifty States. Existing HEA section 101 contains the general institutional education, authorization, public/nonprofit and accreditation framework plus specified additional institutions; the proposal requires a PUBLIC institution and HEA assistance, not every private school or any business offering courses. It does not waive the retained educational-admission qualifications, require admission, provide free tuition, grant an individual federal aid award, or alter visa/admission/removal/work-authorization law. The new section 487(a)(30) requires institutional program participation agreements to comply with section 135A AS APPLICABLE. Existing 487(a) is an institutional initial-and-continuing program-eligibility agreement framework with its subpart-4 exception; this compliance clause is not a replacement of every individual aid-eligibility condition. Existing section 135 already protects resident tuition rates for qualified Federal-service members with the required domicile or permanent duty station, spouses and dependent children, including continued enrollment after duty relocation. Its service categories and effective enrollment dates are retained baseline protections, not proof that this is the first federal resident-rate protection and not deadlines imported into new section 135A. The exact EH prints no special implementation deadline, proof-document procedure or retroactive-refund rule for the new category. This is a whole-bill suspension-and-passage choice and a separate H.R. 6472 episode. No actual institutional compliance, savings, admission or individual nationality determination is established.

The complete H.R. 7744 EH is the whole March 5 House annual DHS proposal with division A annual appropriations and division B lapse-pay/qualified obligation-ratification provisions. Its own sections 3-5 define thisAct references in division A as that DIVISION except where express, explicitly incorporate the January 22 H.R. 7147 explanatory statement for allocation/implementation, and appropriate FY 2026 sums.230(b) uses the corrected DHS-funds-in-this-or-prior-Act scope, not the earlier January as-voted any-other-Act wording. DivisionB 1001 covers the lapse ON OR ABOUT February 13, 2026 (not the February 14 date in the March 27 CRreplacement);1002 directs available 119-37 A/newdivision A personnel pay/allowance/benefit payments under existing 31 US 1341(c);1003 ratifies essential-life/property/orderly-shutdown/otherwise-authorized obligations only IF OTHERWISE IN ACCORD with the referenced Acts. The annual DHS titles would fund existing border processing/security, immigration enforcement, custody and removal, citizenship-services processing and verification, and associated oversight for FY 2026 within a wider DHS package. CBP Operations and Support is $17.727974 billion, with $550 million available through September 30, 2027, mixed customs/trade/travel, UAC transport, air/marine and law-enforcement functions, Harbor Maintenance and user-fee components, and qualified informant, preclearance and Tribal-road uses. CBP procurement/construction is $222.886 million with distinct September 2028 asset and September 2030 construction availability. The final table allocates CBP Ops across Border Security $6.644912 billion, Trade/Travel $6.610801 billion, Integrated Operations $1.730551 billion and Mission Support $2.741710 billion; these are not four independently voted immigration policies or all-person-removal spending. The earlier $650 million CBP-to-FEMA shelter-transfer row has no new Final Bill amount. ICE Ops is $10.036362 billion, including $46.696 million through September 2027, no-year forced-labor funds, qualified HERO/IP-rights/informant/special-operations uses and up to $11.216 million for care, maintenance and repatriation of smuggled aliens UNLAWFULLY PRESENT. The final allocations are HSI $2.591251 billion, ERO $5.453706 billion, Mission Support $1.543711 billion and OPLA $447.694 million. ERO includes Custody $3.838340 billion, Fugitive $165.016 million, Criminal Alien Program $312.835 million, ATD $393.647 million and Transport/Removal $743.868 million. HSI includes many non-immigration investigations; detention and ATD are different uses. These table amounts do not themselves establish actual beds, removals or expenditure. ICE procurement is $5 million through September 2028. USCIS Ops is $122.941 million: $112.566 million Employment Status Verification and $10.375 million Application Processing/backlog reduction in the Final Bill table, not exclusively E-Verify. USCIS has no new Federal Assistance/Citizenship and Integration Grant amount in the final table; previously funded grants and termination-justification reporting are distinct. Existing adjudication-fee authority 1356(m)/(n) and the bill no-required-fee-reduction proviso remain; the separate fee-funded-program table is not an extra new discretionary appropriation. OSEM Ops $316.295 million includes $10 million CRCL, $5 million Citizenship/Immigration Services Ombudsman, no new Immigration Detention Ombudsman allocation, and no new $15 million ATD Case Management Grant allocation; the last two do not abolish their statutory offices or all ATD. OBIM receives $271 million and IDENT/HART procurement $25 million. OIG Ops $257.599 million includes $20 million additional detention inspections through September 2027 and $12.814 million reconciliation-fund oversight.
